On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I should like to

Ontario Indians
ask the Prime Minister or the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs if the attention of the government has been directed to certain reports appearing in the press with regard to what would appear to be a lamentable condition prevailing among the Indians in parts of this country through lack of sufficient care and food. The statement is to the effect that the situation has been brought about in part as a consequence of the cutting down of the appropriations made for the proper care of the Indians. Perhaps my hon. friend the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs is in a position to make a statement.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Superintendent General of Indian Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has couched his question in such general terms that a definite answer is rather difficult to give. I do not know whether he refers to any particular district or to any particular group of Indians, or whether his question applies to all Canada. If he could make his point a little more definite I would be in a better position to answer his question.
I understand the reference is more particularly to the northern Ontario region.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This matter was drawn to my attention, I may say, by an article which appeared in the Toronto Globe with particular reference to that portion of northern Ontario known as the district of Patricia, and the charges outlined in the article were to the effect that the Indians were not being properly looked after. This district, as my right hon. friend knows, is isolated and without means of communication other than by air-plane, by canoe or travel overland. The Indians in that territory are few in number, and in matters of relief we deal with them through the factors of the Hudson's Bay Company and the various missionaries in that area.
In answer to the right hon. gentleman's question I might read portions of a couple of letters which have been received by the Department of Indian Affairs in connection with this matter. The first is a letter from the Trout Lake mission, near Sioux Lookout, which reads as follows:
The plane is expected in next week so I am taking tile opportunity of forwarding you my requisitions for medical and school supplies. I am also sending you the statement of my services as dispenser during the past six months as this is our only winter mail. I have not heard yet as to whether there will be another plane call for the Hudson's Bay Company in June, probably there will.	.
Most likely next week we shall receive the dates for your proposed itinerary next summer.
Now comes the important part of the letter:
The Indians here are keeping very well and happy although fur prices are poor. They have an abundance of country food this winter which is by far the most important for their health and happiness. Please excuse this hasty letter. I have been very busy this winter which has been a very good thing for me as it has kept my mind fully occupied on my work.
That letter is dated February 5, 1932; it is signed by the Reverend Leslie Garrett, and is addressed to H. N. Awrey, of the Department of Indian Affairs, the officer who makes the annual payments during the summer. Then I have an extract from a letter written by Mr. I. W. McCauley, Hudson's Bay Company, Cat Lake Post, Narrow Lake Post Office, Ontario. I may tell my right hon. friend that this office is located near the Cariboo Indians, who are referred to in the Globe article, and who are also known as the Nikip band. This is the extract:
AH the Indians are well up this way and doing fairly well this winter excepting the old people and one woman who is very sick. The Cariboo Indians are also all doing fairly well and are very pleased to hear that you are going to pay them at Cedar Lake this summer.
I do not know whether or not this completely answers the question my right hon. friend has in mind; if not, I may be able to give him further information.

Arising out of the question submitted to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy) by the leader of the opposition-I am sorry I was not in my place at the moment-may I ask the minister whether he would consider sending some airplanes in there with some officers to investigate the condition of the Indians in the Patricia district, where it is reported there have been many deaths as well as considerable suffering.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is a letter only
three weeks' old, saying they were very happy.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the light of information furnished me by the missionary and the factor of the Hudson's Bay Company, I shall have to receive more accurate information before I consider sending airplanes in at this time of year.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is intended to lay upon the table
of the house all orders passed under the authority of the statute to which the hon. gentleman refers. They comprise a considerably large number of orders in council, and the report which the Minister of Labour proposes to table will cover them all. He said yesterday that he hoped to be able to table that report by the end of the week. To postpone until that date consideration of the resolution will work very great hardship upon western Canada. They are dependent upon the ability of the government to enact 
the necessary legislation to make to them advances to permit them to purchase seed grain, the case mentioned by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) being one of them. I propose to make as full an explanation as I think the circumstances demand before seeking an extension of the statute, and if it will be of any interest to the hon. gentleman I may say that I am quite content that every order in council issued under it *should be laid upon the table of the house at the next session of this chamber subsequent to its passing, that is, under the extended order. It is only to meet an emergent situation, full particulars of which we have been endeavouring for weeks to ascertain and which we now have.

maintopic: PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT

I do not know and I do not wish to sail under false colours; I may not know as

Canadian National Railways-Finances
much about temperatures as does my hon. friend, but I do know that the passage of this bill will permit a certain class of petroleum to be used. I was not a member of the house when this act was passed and I cannot of my own knowledge give the information asked for by the hon. member.

The chemists in our

maintopic: PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT

maintopic: PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT

The point raised by
the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) is well taken. The explanatory note reads in part:
The proposal to amend the act to permit the marketing of this product has been submitted to experts of the Department of the Interior and of the Department of National Revenue, who have agreed that the proposed amendment can be made without increasing fire hazard or otherwise interfering with the objects of the act.
Is this amendment to be to the advantage of the consumer or is it to stimulate production? There must be something behind the bill. If the experts have done as the explanatory note says they have done, the minister should be in a position to say who is going to benefit.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 22, to amend the criminal code (cheques without funds and grand juries).

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
This bill is an effort to remedy a difficulty which has been felt for some time, particularly among the commercial people of the country, in regard to cheques issued on banks but dishonoured by them on presentation, in most cases there not being sufficient funds to meet the cheques. The only provision at present in the criminal code which applies to such matters is section 404 which we know as the section respecting false pretences. Under that section it has been very difficult in prosecutions to obtain convictions. It has been held by many magistrates and judges sitting in various courts of the provinces that so long as a man has to his credit in the bank any small sum, he is relieved by that fact of any implications of having obtained money on false pretences, and the number of dishonoured1 cheques has grown to such a tremendous amount in recent years that it is thought some attempt should be made to remedy the difficulty. I think I am 
safe in saying that I have had representations from every province and from every representative board and association asking that some amendment be made to section 404 in an endeavour to obviate this difficulty. The number of cheques which were dishonoured last year by the banks is upwards of 70,000. I received a letter to-day from an hotel manager in Ontario stating that the amount of defaulted cheques which had been received at his hotel last year was $130,000. Subsequently the larger proportion of that amount was of course recovered, but the cheques were actually refused, dishonoured, at the banks. I mention these things to show the extent of the grievance from which the commercial community at the present time suffers.
A bill was introduced last year and a good deal of discussion took place with regard to it, but it wias felt that the bill was not in the best form and the matter was allowed to stand. Since that time the law officers of the Department of Justice have given their best attention to the proposition and have drafted a clause which may to some extent meet the difficulty. The amendment proposed in this bill provides:
In any prosecution under this section-
That is, under the section in respect of false pretences.
-if it be shown that any thing capable of being stolen was obtained by the accused by means of a cheque which, when presented for payment within a reasonable time, was dishonoured on the ground that there were no funds or not sufficient funds on deposit in the bank to the credit of the accused, it shall be presumed that such thing was obtained with fraudulent intent by a false pretence, unless it be established to the satisfaction of the court that when the accused issued such cheque he had reasonable grounds for believing that it would be honoured if presented for payment within a reasonable time after it was issued.
The presumption in such a case is that the issuing of such a cheque was fraudulent, but that presumption may be removed if the accused can establish to the satisfaction of the court that when he issued the cheque he had reasonable grounds ito believe that the bank would pay it. I think if this section is adopted and1 the act is amended and given a fair trial, it will to a very large extent avoid the difficulty from which the commercial community has suffered for so many years. It will not, I am sure, cure every case, but it is a step in the right direction.
The other section of the bill relates merely to the province of British Columbia. The government of that province has asked that

Criminal Code-Cheques Without Funds
wiiat we know as the grand jury system be abolished so far as British Columbia is concerned. .

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Has the minister received any representations from any other bodies than the attorney general of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I think only from the
Attorney General of British Columbia. In the prairie provinces I believe the grand jury system has already been abolished, and British Columbia no doubt is following the lead of the prairie provinces in that respect.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I would suggest that the
following words be inserted after the word " that " in the second line:
Any payment of any account.
This is to cover the case of a man who runs a bill in an hotel, for instance, and pays any account with a worthless cheque.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
This bill is not directed
against cheques issued in payment of debts; it is intended to cover cheques issued for the purpose of obtaining goods. However, when the bill goes into committee, I shall be able to explain it more fully.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in full accord
with the first section of the bill, but frankly, I have grave doubts as to the propriety of the second section and I would ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that, if possible, at a later stage of the bill, he would be good enough not to rush it to completion in order that we may have an opportunity of communicating with various interested bodies in British Columbia. No one knows better than the Minister of Justice the grand jury is an ancient and honourable institution and it provides splendid safeguards in connection with the administration of justice. In addition to the preliminary step of finding a true bill or no bill, our grand ' juries on every occasion in British Columbia make exhaustive investigations into the public institutions of the main centres, and their recommendations have very frequently been adopted as the basis of action. Would the Minister be good enough at a later stage to defer the final stages of the bill in order that we may get in touch with boards of trade, labour organizations, law societies and the bench in British Columbia with regard to their attitude toward this particular section?

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.
On section 1.-Obtaining by false pretence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Before I overlook the
matter, let me say in reply to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, that I shall be glad to let the bill stand for third reading until he has had an opportunity of communicating with the various bodies in British Columbia whom he mentioned. Personally I am strongly in favour of the grand jury system, and I hesitate very much to agree to its abolition in any province. Yet we must remember that the administration of justice is left in the hands of the provinces and the various provinces make representations that the cost of the grand jury system is very serious, particularly at the present time. I liked the old grand jury of twenty-four, now reduced in the province of Ontario to twelve. That reduction took place for the purpose of saving expense. Now the proposal in the west seems to be to do away with grand juries altogether. I think that they were a valuable part of the administration of the law, and not only in regard to the administration of criminal justice, but grand juries took a general survey of their immediate surroimdings and of the public institutions in their neighbourhood and their reports to judges, and afterwards to governments, were very often very valuable sources of information. I for one do not like to see the system abandoned, but when a responsible officer of the government of a province makes a request for the abolition of that system on the ground of the saving of expense I think perhaps it is our duty to give serious consideration to that request, and as grand juries have been abolished in the prairie provinces, perhaps it would not be unreasonable to grant the same request in British Columbia.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Did they ever have grand juries in the prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: No, they have never been adopted there, and the administration of the law seems to be quite satisfactory there without them. Perhaps it would be reasonable to grant the request of British Columbia. However, I shall be only too glad to let the matter stand until we hear from various public bodies in British Columbia as to what they think of the proposal.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
The point I wanted to
raise a little while ago was this: This morning I received a letter from a client of mine saying that someone had received money to give to his client, and instead of turning that money over to his client the individual put the money in the bank and made payment by cheque. Later when the cheque was presented
670	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Cheques Without Funds
for payment there were no funds in the bank to meet it. That happens quite often. I think there should be some provision in the law covering such a practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I am afraid that this
proposed amendment would not cover the case cited by my hon. friend. That is a case where a man obtains money without cheque at all and subsequently issues a cheque to cover the debt. The clause before us applies only to persons who obtain any property that is capable of being stolen, and obtain it by the issuing of a cheque which subsequently turns out to be bad. The mere fact of giving a worthless cheque in payment of an old account does not injure anybody.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
This was not an old
account. Suppose a lawyer receives the sum of one hundred dollars to give to a client of his, puts the money into his bank and makes payment by cheque, and the cheque later is not accepted by the bank. There should be a provision in the law to cover such cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
That is already covered
by our law. That is the conversion of property to his own use, which is a criminal act on the part of the lawyer. But he did not obtain the money by means of a worthless cheque.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I remember well that
one of the bodies that were most active in asking for legislation of this kind was the hotelkeepers' association. The hotelkeepers always represented that in various states of the American union the hotelkeepers are protected against N.S.F. cheques, but if I read the section aright, the hotelkeepers will not be protected by the present amendment because when a man issues a cheque for his board at a hotel, it is not in payment of something that is capable of being stolen at the time he makes payment because he has already eaten his board when he gives the cheque. So this will not meet the case, if I understand it aright.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
No, I think it is very
doubtful if it will meet the case of a hotel bill, any more than any other bill. This only covers an actual transaction where the goods are obtained by fraudulent means through the issue of a worthless cheque. A man who has run up a board bill for a week or two, or a month or two, and settles with a worthless cheque is not obtaining goods on false pretences; he is refusing to pay for them.

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

I am sorry the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) did not speak in English, because he made it clear that this short text of law is much more important and

Criminal Code-Cheques Without Funds
capable of more far reaching consequences than most members realize. Of course, it may be very impertinent for a layman and an ignorant fellow to interfere in a discussion between legal lights. However, in my few years of the study of British law I have understood that the basic principle of penal legislation, both in Canada and Great Britain, has been that every accused man shall be held innocent until he is proved guilty, and that the duty of the government or-may I enlarge the word-the duty of all representatives in authority, whether in legislative or judiciary capacities, is, not to protect crooks, but at least to give accused persons a fair chance.
Under the proposed new text of law I find the following most striking expression:
any thing capable of being stolen . . .

My Scottish friends would be reminded of the heroic deeds of old Scotch caterans. But that is not the important part; what I object to most of all is that it shall be "presumed" that such thing was obtained with fraudulent intent. That is the point which I think deserves consideration, and to which I object. Since the war, probably because in this country as elsewhere the war enhanced the activities and energies of many people, many fraudulent processes have developed; and I realize the desire of the government and especially of the Minister of Justice to help honest people protect themselves against crooks. On the other hand, however, in this as in other respects let us beware that the remedy does not open the door to worse evils than those we wish to correct. I think the old British principle of not unduly protecting the accused, but of at least giving him a chance to defend himself, is one from which we should not depart without much hesitation.
It happened that while I was on the train yesterday I heard a country merchant dis-41761-43
cussing this very bill with his friend. That was the first I had heard of it. Let us take a case
apart from hotels altogether. Suppose I issue a cheque in payment of a small bill: under the law as it stands now, if that cheque comes back as having not sufficient funds, can I be arrested and prosecuted?

in payment of a former purchase there are no

false pretences. The position of the creditor is not affected in that case; you do not make it worse. You have simply given him a bad cheque. But if you obtain goods by issuing a cheque for which there are no funds you are obtaining those goods under false pretences.

on summary conviction in this case. This is a crime. When a man is arrested on complaint, under the criminal code the matter cannot be settled civilly. Taking that view, that
man can be arrested and it is a criminal matter. That is how I interpret it. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

subtopic: CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS-GRAND JURY SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
The objection one often meets with before the courts in matters of this kind is that the criminal courts refuse to allow themselves to be used as collection agencies. In this case it seems to me that the accused is placed at a disadvantage. The ordinary evil-minded man, the criminal, steals a certain sum of money from someone and is brought to trial and all he has to do is to sit back and the crown has to prove his guilt, whereas in this circumstance a man might be of the most innocent mind and might issue a cheque on 41761-431
the strength of one deposited from someone else. That cheque is returned from the bank as having no funds, and the cheque he has issued is therefore no good. He is haled before the courts and has to defend himself, and the presumption is against him, the same as in automobile cases, in the province of Quebec at least. A man charged with a breach of the automobile law has to prove that he is not guilty. This legislation is of the same kind. A man, whether he is innocent or not, is taken before the courts and has to prove that he had no intention of fraudulently issuing the cheque, whereas the ordinary criminal, as I have pointed out, has nothing to do but to sit back and allow the crown to prove its case against him. It has been asked for
very generally throughout Canada by the retail merchants' associations in the various provinces, some chambers of commerce and some boards of trade. Innumerable correspondents have asked for it, including the hotelkeepers' association. I have had only one or two letters, not from the association but from hotelkeepers; my colleagues have also received letters, and I know that my good friend who brought the matter up last year has been deluged with them. The object of the bill is, if possible, to put a stop to the issuing of worthless cheques. I do not think that the people who issue such cheques should be encouraged or surrounded with all sorts of safeguards. The honest man will have no difficulty whatever under the bill. The man who parts with his goods or services should have some recourse. I think the bill should be given a trial. In spite of it the practice will continue, but I think this legislation will help. At any rate, the idea is, as far as possible, to put an end to what is a very reprehensible practice. As regards the criticism that this is a bad time to enforce it, I do not think that we can ask the merchants and gas dealers of the country to bear the costs of providing for those who are in need at the present time, and that is what this argument amounts to. A man goes into a store and obtains certain goods, and no matter how hard up he may be, if he gets the purchase on the strength of a cheque which he knows is not going to be honoured he is guilty of a transaction which no one can justify. You cannot ask the retail merchant to bear the loss. If the purchaser is honest and has reason to believe that the bank will honour the cheque, if he has a balance and has a right

to overdraw, all lie has to do is to explain that to the court and that will constitute reasonable grounds and he will be acquitted.

A false pretence is a representation, either by words or otherwise, of a matter of fact either present or past, which representation is known to the person making it to be false, and which is made with a fraudulent intent to induce the person to whom it is made to act upon such representation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it seems to
me to be a professional obsession of every legal man to look at these matters from the point of view of the crook. Do they never consider it from the other side? Do they never think of the small store-keeper who ha? been stung by this wholesale and widespread system of extortion? We all know that the ultimate sufferer is the general public because the expenses of the store-keeper must be paid. A great deal of the objection to this bill has been raised by those who innocently or perhaps inadvertently ignore the provisions for the protection of the accused. To my mind the words "reasonable grounds" should take care of most of these objections. The popular conception of British jurisprudence is, as has been stated, that a man must be considered innocent until he is proved guilty. That has a fine sound, somewhat *similar to the demand for British justice which we hear at times. My experience has been that when a man demands British justice he is often after something more than is coming to him. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has said, our laws are full of provisions whereby a man faced with
IMr. Guthrie.]
a set of condemnatory or suspicious circumstances has to give a reasonable explanation. This morning the marine and fisheries committee was dealing with the amendment to an act, which provided time and time again the onus of proof shall be placed upon the accused. The same applies to our provincial liquor acts and to the criminal code.
The provisions of this bill will not apply, as some people seem to think they will, to the small business man who draws a cheque inadvertently or who believes that his bank will give him one more chance. That man can quite readily and without any trouble prove his innocence, but the intention of this bill is to get at the fly-by-night who makes it his profession-call it that if you will- or occupation to go around from town to town passing worthless cheques. This man generally comes to the store-keeper on Saturday afternoon; he is always well dressed and has every appearance of having millions behind him. He goes in and buys an article without kicking about the price, gives a cheque in payment and receives the balance in cash. This is the sort of man it is intended to get after.
Let us forget the crook for a moment and consider the 70,000 bad cheques which were issued last year. What were the protest fees alone on those cheques which the storekeeper or individual had to pay? We should consider the upset to business which this sort of thing brings about. Hon. gentlemen have asked if there has been any demand for this amendment and the minister has indicated that he has received a number of letters and petitions in connection therewith. Never since I have been in parliament have I received so many letters and applications from individuals and organizations requesting legislation. These have come not only from my own province but from the maritime provinces as well. I have received letters from Montreal, Quebec, and Winnipeg and other cities throughout the dominion. The writers stated that they noticed I was taking up this bill, and they wished me God-speed. They urged the extreme necessity of this amendment and stated that there would be no danger of injustice being done.
There is a great need for this amendment. The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) quoted a section of the criminal code which he thought applied. I have not the section before me but as I understand it, the section under which offences of this kind are tried only requires the accused to say that when he issued the cheque in question he

Unemployment-Mr. Fournier
hoped that some unknown benefactor would pay money into his bank account before the cheque was presented. He might know perfectly well that he had no money in his account or that he had only a few cents, he might know perfectly well his credit was beyond redemption in every way but, under the present act, it is not necessary for him to prove anything, all he has to do is to sit back and say, "When I issued that cheque I had no intention of defrauding." The prosecution has to prove what was in that man's mind at the time he issued the cheque, and that explains the small number of convictions obtained.
Perhaps this bill does not go far enough, but I believe it takes ample care of the man who innocently overdraws his account, as I have done myself. It makes an attempt to stop the practice of issuing bad cheques. This practice increases when times are bad, because then a man will go into forms of crookedness which he would not otherwise consider. The evil is growing and protection should be given to the store-keeper, and in that way we will help poor people because it is the store-keeper to whom we turn when we need a little credit. For the protection of all we should deal vigilantly with these professional crooks.

who has been on many occasions the victim of these cheque artists, I believe I can speak feelingly on this subject. I am in agreement with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and I assure him that his bill will meet with the general approval of the people whom I represent in this house. The time has arrived when we should stop this ever-increasing practice of issuing worthless cheques. I see no reason why fraud should be condoned, particularly by this parliament.
A situation has developed in the rural sections in connection with the marketing of goods. maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the adjournment of the house last Tuesday I had reviewed briefly the different means by which the government had tried to relieve unemployment. I mentioned relief work, direct relief, raising of tariffs and economy. By the first means the governments throughout the dominion spent the sum of $70,000,000 in 1930 to relieve unemployment, the federal share of this amount being around $18,000,000. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) stated that this amount of money had helped 334,000 people during 1930. The people that were helped received a little over
7,000,000 days of work. By going a little further we find that each person who was helped received from this fund of $70,000,000 about twenty-three days' work in 1930. By dividing the amount spent by the number of days, we find that each day's work given during that year to the unemployed cost the country $10.
It is estimated that the amount which will have been spent in 1931 will be $60,000,000, the share of the federal government being about $28,000,000. This has helped 285,000 people and given them to January 1, 1932, eleven days' work per person. If you make the same division you will find that in 1931 it still cost the government $10 to give one day's work to each of those 285,000 persons who obtained relief work. In those two years there has been spent on relief work the sum of $130,000,000.
The second means by which the government tried to relieve unemployment was direct relief. I have no figures for 1931, but I have found figures concerning 1930. In that year over $7,000,000 was spent for direct relief, helping 438,777 single men and heads of families. The amount contributed by the federal gov-
Unemployment-Mr. Fournier

ernment was $2,174,000. I would like the house to note that in 1930 more people benefited under relief or the dole than by relief work.
The third means which the government had in mind to help relieve unemployment was the raising of tariffs. Tariffs were raised during the sessions of 1930 and 1931. Their effects cannot all be known at the present time, but one thing is sure and that is that unemployment, instead of decreasing during those two years, kept on increasing. Not only did general unemployment increase, but we find that employees in manufactures were less numerous during those last two years than they were before. I have under my hand figures showing the employment situation in manufacturing in the month of October for different years, as follows:
October	Employment
1926	 104-6
1928	 115-7
1930		 107-8
1931		 91-8
This was the third means used by the government to relieve unemployment.
The fourth means was economy, which was to be practised along the whole line. Economy may be practised in various ways to relieve unemployment, but the way it should be practised is rather to keep people who have jobs working than to have them lose their positions. These four means were tried throughout the country and to-day we can to a certain extent judge the results so far as employment is concerned. In September, 1930, after the Minister of Labour had made an inquiry concerning the number of unemployed in Canada, it was found that 117,000 people were out of work. In 1931, after this legislation in regard to unemployment was put into force, it was found that the number of unemployed had risen from 117,000 to 350,000, and certain papers state that this year the number of unemployed has risen to 450,000.
May I say a few words concerning the city of Hull just across the river. In September, 1930, after the inquiry was conducted there, it was found there were 1,500 people unemployed, and during that year the municipal council, the provincial government and the federal government spent some $350,000 to relieve unemployment. This year they are spending $500,000, of which the provincial and federal governments are furnishing 80 per cent. These amounts were spent on public works just to create jobs without bringing into being any new wealth in our city. It was just a kind of dole given under the form of work. By direct relief we have spent this year some $75,000, part furnished by this government and part by the municipality and the provincial government. Are there any more employed

in the city of Hull? The last figures available show that during the month of January the number of unemployed was 2,000, and of that number about 400 were working for the city one week out of four, leaving the balance of about 1,600 people without work or working only a few days a week. No industry in Hull is working full time at the present. The largest industry is the E. B. Eddy Company which works only three or four days a week. Other industries, such as J. R. Booth Limited, Woods Manufacturing Company Limited, and Grant-Holden-Graham Limited are working on the same basis. Surely the government could find some means to help these unemployed at the present time.
Instead of the number of the unemployed decreasing, we are suffering from another ill which is created by the government itself. I am informed that lately notice has been sent by the Department of Public Works to seventy or seventy-five pepole that their services will be no longer required after the first of April of this year. Yesterday I received a visit from one of those men who was employed by the Public Works department. He had been working there for the last eight years. He is the father of nine children. Although when he got this job it was not permanent, he was a good enough employee to hold it for eight years. He had bought a little home in the city and had paid for it in part. He stiE owes on that place about $1,200 under a mortgage. Yesterday he received notice that his services would be no more required after the first of April. What is he to do now, under present conditions? On Friday the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), speaking on the resolution in regard to reducing salaries, began by stating that the civil service was overmanned. The next day orders were given, I suppose to every department, and! especially to the Department of Public Works, to throw out this surplus of men. I would just ask the government if the time is weE chosen to dismiss from the public employ people who have small jobs as labourers ,or as tradesmen. I sought information as to whether this man was doing useful work at the department, and it was stated that he was at work every hour; he was occupied the whole time. It is hard to believe that there is any reason for throwing out at the end of this month some seventy-five employees. I wonder if the matter was ever considered on its merits, if it was ever thought that these people might have families to look after and that the married ones might be given a chance instead of perhaps keeping on some single men.

Unemployment-Mr. Fournier
Another case came to my knowledge of a man who has been working thirty years with the Public Works department. He received notice yesterday that from ithe first of April next his services will not be required. In that department alone the dismissals are going to affect seventy-five families in the cities of Ottawa and Hull. Just add that figure to those I have already cited and you will realize that the help we have received from this government for the unemployed does not amount to very much.
The schemes that I have mentioned for helping the unemployed would seem to be very costly. If this country has to spend ten dollars for every day's work it provides for an unemployed man, I really think some other way should ibe found of giving help to those who are needing work. We must remember that when these schemes were put into operation trade was diminishing and revenues were falling, and we did not have sufficient revenue to carry on the whole administration. It was necessary, therefore, to borrow money to put these schemes into operation. The sum of $130,000,000 which I have mentioned-borrowed money-was added to the indebtedness of Canada, plus nearly $6,500,000 for interest which will have to foe paid.
In the city of Ottawa one would think -that unemployment would Ibe unknown, but in February last, I read the following news item in the Ottawa Citizen, written to show that this plague of unemployment is prevalent in every city and town, and that Ottawa is no exception. It reads:
Work For Ottawa Women
Yesterday in Ottawa, some devoted members of the Local Council of Women opened a work room where destitute women can be given an opportunity to earn a few dollars weekly. The plan is to give out sewing and mending work. On the first day more than 130 women applied. Some are receiving temporary relief through the welfare bureau, but they are women who want work rather than a charitable ration of food.
It is surely a reflection on established things in Canada, in this capital city where the political wisdom of the nation is regularly assembled, that there should be decent Canadian women so beset, so trapped near the margin of existence. Many have vainly applied, day after day, at the employment office: some are bravely trying to keep a home together, to provide for young children.
The city council has granted $1,500 for the work, for the purchase of material and the payment of wages. It is a pitifully small amount; but the minister of public works, Hon. H. A. Stewart, has granted the use of a vacant work room. Ottawa has cause to he grateful to the thoughtful women of the local council who have started this measure of relief.
This welfare bureau, opening up some sort of room to give mending and sewing to women,
had 130 women apply the first day for work. That will give some idea of conditions in the city of Ottawa, where so many people are in the employ of the government-or were up to this time; for soon there will not be so many. There are nearly fifteen thousand civil servants in Ottawa, and their dependents number from fifty to sixty thousand, yet we find women having to go to the welfare bureau for food or work, though naturally they prefer work to charity.
In September, 1930, the government thought that this would be a normal depression. As my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) said, we do not yet know exactly what a normal depression is, or even an abnormal one, but by this time the government has certainly found out that this is no ordinary depression. The Minister of Labour stated last Tuesday that it was not a normal depression; that if it had been, the measures adopted by the government would have cured unemployment and the depression. Now that the government knows that this is not a normal depression we are waiting to see what means it is going to adopt to deal with the situation. We do not believe they will go on borrowing money for two years up to $130,000,000 to carry on schemes that do not seem to be sound, because remember that more than half the unemployed did not receive any assistance at all. There are certain classes of the unemployed who did not come under any of these schemes. The labouring classes and trades people were helped, but what about clerks in stores and bookkeepers and office help employed in commercial houses? These people received no assistance at all under any of the different schemes of the government, and they are suffering probably more than the labouring classes. If the civil servants in this city are to be thrown out of employment at the rate of seventy-five or one hundred a week they will help to swell the ranks of the unemployed, and they can hardly do the work that the ordinary labouring man has to do. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that we are very anxious to know what steps the government is going to take in the near future to cope with this situation.
May I as a new member humbly suggest that the government give more assistance to those who desire to go back to the land, and that before they do so they let them know that they are not going on a farm to commercialize agriculture as it has been commercialized in the west.
The farmers in the province of Quebec are not suffering as much as they are in other parts of this dominion, it is for the simple reason that in our province a farmer living on the land has this in mind: first to find
Unemployment-Mr. Fournier

sustenance for his family and himself and, secondly, if there is anything left over, to give a little education to his children. He does not go on the farm with the idea of getting rich quick. He wants to make a comfortable living on the land and to provide his family with a certain standard of living, but he has not in his mind what I seem to notice in certain members from the west who come from rural constituencies. They have only one idea in agriculture and that is to raise wheat. Outside of wheat they sow nothing, and when the wheat crop fails or they cannot sell their grain, they come to the government and say: We want a bonus of five cents a bushel. The eastern members have not raised their voices on this five cent bonus. We think the western provinces should be helped, but in the province of Quebec we have not been asking for five cents a bushel bonus on potatoes or on oats. We are holding up our heads in this depression. Some day we might find it necessary to come here and ask for five cents a bushel on some product or another. What we are asking now is for a little more help for those who have no work at all. If you cannot give them work, you are going to give them charity. I do not care what the Prime Minister says about the dole, but people must not be allowed to starve. If they are not given work they must be given some sort of dole or assistance, and if they are going to starve, they will put up some fight. Every Saturday in the city of Hull some seven or eight hundred people gather at the city hall asking first for work, and when they cannot get work they ask for something to eat. If they cannot get something to eat for themselves, they ask it for their children. Certainly during this session there will have to be some new scheme on the part of the government to help us a little more. I am not painting this picture any worse than it is; I am not saying that everybody in Hull is starving, but I am attempting to show that those people are waiting for action from this government because it said it would do something for them. They have been led to believe that they might expect help. I believe, it would be the proper time for these unemployed to repeat some of the statements made by the leaders of the present government before July 1930. I quote:
They play with the lives of men and women. What for? Do they realize there are lives that they are playing with, food for wives and children, hunger?
And this also:
However blind he may be to your future and deaf to your present needs, surely he cannot stop his ears with smug complacence and self esteem to the cry that carries across
[Mr. Fournier.}
the nation-the cry of the destitute and hungry, the cry of mothers and fathers and little children who call for us as Christians and as Canadians to heal their pain.
I do not know if those words were true in 1930 when the statement was made; they were not true at that time in my city. It is true to-day, however, in the city of Hull, and I beg this government to take some steps to alleviate the situation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the last remarks of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier), I quite agree. The first consideration of this government, and of all provincial and municipal governments, should be to relieve the situation in congested cities by inducing as many people as possible to go back to the land, provided -and I insist on these two conditions-provided the proper kinds of lands are made available, and that the people sent to the country are capable of making a living on the land. Otherwise any such movement would be waste effort.
My purpose in rising this afternoon, contrary to my original intention, is to explain, in case I am not here when the vote is taken, why I cannot associate myself with the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan). After the general elections of 1930, I came back to this house more than ever decided to dissociate myself from any party movement directed for the sole or main purpose of creating party advantage. I quite understand the state of mind of my Liberal friends. No doubt they were defeated owing to circumstances and conditions over which they had no control and, may I say, to the shameless exploitation of those circumstances by their opponents. But now, in the year 1932, the people of Canada are expecting from all of us, whether we be Liberal, Conservative, or Independent, something greater than bickerings over the past election. There will be ample opportunities for my Liberal friends to bring to task their opponents. At the present time, during this session, the people of Canada expect from us something practical by way of economic reconstruction.
Turning to this motion-I was going to say this speech in the form of a motion- proposed by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River, I must say that with the sole exception of the last paragraph I find it contains nothing which will help either parliament or the people. I pass over the recital composed of quotations from speeches by the present leader of the government. If I am not mistaken those same quotations were

Unemployment-Mr. Bourassa
used at least three times by the leader of the opposition; they are on record in Hansard, and the people of Canada no doubt have read them. I do not think, however, they would be disposed to read them very often. With all due respect to both sides of the house, may I say that to some people those quotations appear senseless enough, and others believe that the leader of the opposition has said enough about them. The press of the country, irrespective of party, has shewn its keen sense of criticism-and I use the word "criticism" in the proper sense-by omitting in their reports of debates the reproduction of all those paragraphs. My hon. friend from Ivenora-Rainy River and his associates might learn that even as a vote-catcher these fourth-time recitals of quotations from speeches do not carry very much weight.
Let us now analyze the motion, paragraph by paragraph.
First, I read the following:
That whereas notwithstanding the government demanded and received from parliament unlimited authority to use the resources of the treasury of Canada to such an extent as the government deemed expedient for the purpose of relief of unemployment, the measures taken by the government to eliminate unemployment have proven wholly inadequate and ineffective;
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is too far-fetched. If the statement had been made that the measures were not as effective and as adequate as they might have been, and if the criticism had been directed to a certain laxity or abuse in the administration of enactments arising out of the indefinite powers granted by this parliament last year, I might have agreed. But to go the length of saying that everything the government has done in the last twelve months has been "wholly inadequate and ineffective," is going beyond the measure of justice, fair play and truth; and I do not think such sentiments will be endorsed by fair minded people in Canada, to whatever party they may belong.
Therefore, let us pass over that clause and come to the second:
That the measures adopted by the government have involved an expenditure of public moneys out of all proportion to the employment provided;
Again we find here partial exaggeration. Undoubtedly a great deal of the moneys spent by this government, as well as by various provincial and municipal governments, to cure or relieve unemployment, has been lost or misapplied. What proportion of federal, provincial or municipal funds has not been used to the best advantage I am not prepared to say, and I do not think any hon. member, not even the hon. member for
Kenora-Rainy River, is capable at the present time of stating the amount of money misspent by various bodies.
I now come to the next paragraph, and my statements in connection therewith will apply also to the following one:
That owing to lack of proper supervision and organization there has been partisan administration of the moneys provided by parliament for the benefit of those who were the most in need of work;
This is absolutely true, Mr. Speaker. There has been a partisan spirit evinced-I will not say by the federal, the provincial or municipal governments, but by some representatives of those three authorities. Of such abuse, the city of Montreal offers to-day a most striking example. As the citizens of Montreal are proud to boast, that city is the largest in Canada, and therefore the one containing the largest number of paupers and unemployed. The municipal government of that city is headed by a man much discussed, but certainly very clever and energetic; I refer to Mayor Houde. He is a Conservative in politics, the late leader of the provincial opposition in the Quebec legislature, and now on the eve of his reelection, if he' can secure it, as mayor of Montreal. The federal government is represented in Montreal by a federal commissioner, Mr. Gravel, and the provincial authorities by their own commissioner, Mr. Perrier. We may view the whole situation as it was painted or exhibited last week by a meeting between the authorities. The provincial commissioner, Mr. Perrier, made the charge, point blank, that the aider-men were making use of the administration of relief funds for purposes of reelection in the month of April, rather than to alleviate the sufferings of the people. There may be some truth in that. Then the mayor launched a furious attack against the federal commissioner, Mr. Gravel, charging him with attempts at corruption in order to have contracts made in favour of friends of the federal government, and to those charges Mr. Gravel issued a denial.
How much is true in any of those accusations I do not know. This I know, however: at. the present time, in Montreal, there are works and contracts, worth some $500,000, which are paralyzed because of this partisan, narrow-minded attitude of the representatives of the three governing bodies. But I am not prepared by my vote to charge this government with being solely responsible for that state of things, although heaven knows I am not particularly friendly with them as a government.
I do not like to introduce small, county politics into this debate: but there are un-

Unemployment-Mr. Bourassa
employed people in my constituency. Relief works have been started by the federal and provincial governments. I cannot blame this government for having made it a previous condition to the granting of federal aid to local works that, first, the municipalities and then the provinces should share in the cost, and I fail to see that my Liberal friends can throw stones at the government for having done that. I well remember, when sitting on the other side and, occupying towards the Liberal government about the same position I occupy to-day towards the Conservative government, only with a little more sympathy, hearing the Prime Minister of that day, the present leader of the opposition, state that not only the main but practically the sole responsibility for the solving of the problem of unemployment was on the municipalities and the provinces. In those days he was right. I then told him however that he was blind to the rapid growth of the evil which was soon to get beyond the power of 'Solution by either municipalities or provinces.
In Canada, at the present time, as at every other time past or to come, no government can shelter itself behind a narrow interpretation of the law in order to avoid the fulfilment of a national duty. I agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that this is a national duty; but national duty in Canada must be performed according to the broad spirit as well as the rightly interpreted letter of the constitution. In Canada we have three powers, the federal, the provincial and the municipal. In a matter of this kind a national duty cannot be effectively performed unless those three authorities cooperate in the solution of the problem. Things should not be done in order to help the mayor of a certain town secure reelection, to help the government of a certain province secure the confidence of the electors, or to help friends of the federal government make use of their influence to secure contracts in different places. Public good and general results should be the sole aim.
Accusations have been launched, and others probably will be made during this debate by Liberal members, that some representatives of the Conservative governments, the federal or the provincial in Ontario or British Columbia, have made use of this relief act and these relief funds to help their friends. As a counterpart to that, I may tell the house that I have received letters from most reliable men in my constituency-which I may say covers two provincial divisions-complaining that in the carrying on of work subsidized by

the Conservative government at Ottawa no Conservative voter need apply, because the patronage is under the control of the provincial Liberal member. I know that personally I suggested a certain piece of work, useful in itself and capable of rendering service not only this year but for many years to come, in a certain municipality. I was told by the director of national relief at Ottawa that he was prepared to recommend that work to the minister, provided the province of Quebec approved of it. Application was made to Quebec, but that application was refused because the local member did not like the people who advocated this work. Mind you, those people were Liberals, but they were not orthodox Liberals in the eyes of the local member. The Quebec government did not approve the suggestion; therefore the money from Ottawa was not sent; therefore the people are unemployed and living on charity. This all happened because of political partisanship, but this time on the part of Liberals.
So I think it is about time we in this house, who seriously wish to accomplish something for our country, should cease to talk about this grave matter from the narrow point of view of political partisanship. Mind you, I do not reproach either my hon. friends to my right or my hon. friends to my left with being party men. They have been elected as such. But I do claim that there is a time to advocate party measures and a tame to forget them. It is done every day on other matters; why should it not 'be done in connection with this matter, which has been rightly called by the bon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, and is so described in the motion, .the most important problem we have to solve?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: If we give suggestions in all earnestness and the government refuse to accept those suggestions, what can we do?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
That is not the question;
I was speaking about the paragraph in the motion having to do with partisan administration, and I was proving that there is partisan spirit in the administration of the federal funds, of the provincial funds under the government of the dear friend of my hon. friend from Temiscouata, Mr. Taschereau, and of the municipal funds in Montreal under Mayor Houde. I have given names; I have given foots, and1 that is all I have to say for the present in that regard. Under such a system, perhaps unavoidable with our political organization, there is bound to 'be a large degree of maladministration in the distribution of those funds and in the approval or disapproval of certain works.

Unemployment-Mr. Bourassa
Now let us consider what works should be undertaken. In this regard there is bound to be a great variety of opinions. For example, my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River, last year and again this year, strenuously advocated the construction of a national highway in order to give work to the unemployed. I did not approve then, and I do not approve now, of that idea; it is one of the things for which I would be disposed to blame not particularly this government, but the governments of Ontario and Quebec as well. The view I 'have expressed both inside and outside this house-more particularly outside-with regard to this work is, that although we have as our immediate object the alleviation of unemployment, something else has to be considered. First, we cannot hope to cure unemployment, or to end unemployment, by government aid only. That sort of talk may be used at election time, but we do not talk seriously all the time during an election. Now, however, that we are attempting to do something serious, we can alleviate unemployment by giving work of a temporary nature or of a permanent nature, work capable of producing some good now but of doubtful use in the future, or work capable of being useful for years to come. I claim, sir, that the spending of millions on the construction of a great automobile highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific is largely wasting money. First of all, the construction of roads in winter time in a country like ours takes three times as much money as the construction of roads in summer; and this applies to the construction not only of that great road but of all roads that have been built in the province of Quebec under the joint approval of the federal and provincial governments. Secondly, we have to consider the whole problem of transportation. A commission has been appointed by this government with a view to solving the great railway problem of Canada; and while our railways are complaining of the competition to which they are subject from highway traffic, this government and the two provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec are spending millions to increase that competition and decrease the earnings of the railways, thereby rendering more difficult the solution of this problem, one of the most difficult which faces this government or any government that may succeed it. I claim that in this regard all that should have been done-and it is not too late yet to consider that humble but more practical solution of our highway problem-was to help, in all the provinces, the various small sections of the country that have no proper communication
with the railway centres to carry their produce over good roads to the railway stations and to bring back what goods they import over the railways; in other words, to reduce the cost of local transportation. That would have been far better than building a highway at a cost of millions upon millions of dollars to attract American tourists, who in any event would not deprive themselves of the pleasure of coming to Canada and enjoying the hospitality of our various liquor commissions. They would not, I say, forego that pleasure merely because they could not drive straight through from Prince Rupert to Sydney, but might be obliged to make crochets, going through from one dry state to one free .province, and from one free province to one dry state. I am sure they would enjoy, their trip all the more, taking that roundabout course, and there would be less danger to passersby than if they started from a wet province and went all through the continent, east to west or west to east, from one wet province to another.
The same criticism I make against that great and costly highway project, as a competitor with our railways, I make against the project first launched in the Montreal city council and then approved of by the provincial authorities and finally endorsed by this government: I mean the building of a boulevard from one end of the island of Montreal to the other. There will be spent on this the sum of perhaps ten million dollars-to whose profit? To the profit of speculators who some years ago purchased land which they were not able to sell before prices were slaughtered and who, having these vacant lands, are now getting them expropriated by the municipal council to be paid for by the province and the dominion. And they call that a relief of unemployment, while at the present time, in that great city of Montreal, we have at least 75,000 human beings, men, women and children, who are living under conditions that are not fit for animals! Instead of devoting ten or fifteen million dollars to the building of a boulevard for the sake of land speculators and for people who are in a hurry to traverse the whole length of the island at forty miles an hour, would it not have been better to spend this money, municipal money, provincial money and federal money, in improving the permanent conditions of the poor people of Montreal, the dwellings, so that after this time of depression had passed, they might be in a condition, mental and physical, that would enable them to be of service to the city, to the province and to the state?
Unemployment-Mr. Bourassa

I cannot lay the blame for this piece of foolishness, for this social crime, at the door of this government. The first guilty party was the municipal council; the second guilty party was the provincial government; and I will admit the third guilty party is this government-guilty of having granted a share of federal subsidies to that scheme.
