speechtext: There is a small difference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Yes, a small difference; you are all partakers in the misdeed, though in varying degrees. I leave the hon. gentleman to settle that himself or to submit it to some board of arbitration. But I cite that as an example to show my unwillingness to support the resolution as it stands; because if we undertake now-and I do not think it is the proper time-to pass judgment upon all that has been done in the way of misappropriation or misapplication in regard to relief funds, then it is not just to take only one of the parties concerned without the others.
I may say in passing that this would be ample justification for the acceptance by the government and by the house of the suggestion twice made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), that this whole question, broad as it is and involving as it does, not only moral responsibilities, but the financial support of the various authorities who have no jurisdiction one over another, should have been placed in the hands of a national commission to which appointees should have been nominated by the federal government, by the provincial government and perhaps by some of the larger municipalities.
Coming now to the question of wages, I am afraid I must differ both from my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan)

and from my friends who represent labour in the house. Speaking generally, I agree with them that it is dangerous to allow, under circumstances such as we are faced with at present, the possibility of lower wages becoming an established fact. But then I invoke again the old axiom, salus populi suprema lex esto. There is no law which does not call for exceptions at times. Now, what is the need at the present time? Everyone is agreed on that. It is to enable the largest number of people to work for their livelihood instead of living by alms, by hand to mouth charity. Given that condition, I ask my hon. friends who represent the Labour party to consider a municipality in the mountains of the province of Quebec-and there are hundreds of such municipalities-where the people can get food, lodging and fuel at about one-quarter of what it costs individuals who are waiting for work in Montreal, Quebec, Sherbrooke and Three Rivers. Are the people in such districts in any worse position if they are paid a wage which will enable them to purchase the necessities of life on the same margin, as between money earned and money spent, as the man in Montreal? What does it matter so long as they get the same in quantity and quality for their maintenance? A man earns three dollars and spends it in the purchase of what he and his family need. Another gets only two dollars, but with those two dollars is able to purchase exactly the same quantity and quality of staple goods required by his family. What difference does it make? That is the situation. I take full responsibility, before my Labour friends and before the labourers and farmers of my constituency, for having strongly advised the representative of the federal government, the director of the relief fund, to change the regulations last year.
Let me give an illustration. In my constituency there is a fairly large village where there were some forty or fifty unemployed. These men used to go to the shanties to work six or eight months and then come back to the village and perform occasional work for the remainder of the year. Last year, those men were idle; so the municipality applied to the provincial government for relief, and a certain piece of work was approved. This suggestion was sent to Ottawa, where it was approved by the federal authorities. The municipality then made a calculation to see what it would cost to make use of the federal and provincial help, and found out that it would cost more than it would cost them unaided to help their own people in their own way. Appeals were made to the people in the village that they do everything to help. They were asked to

Unemployment-Mr. Bourassa
give work to a man for eight or ten days although they had no special need for it. They were told if they paid so much, the council would pay so much and the taxation rate would remain at its then level. Had they subordinated the scheme to the conditions imposed by the provincial and federal governments, even with the money received from Ottawa and Quebec, they would have had to spend more money and the municipality would have been in a worse condition.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is right, as are others, when he says that the manner in which the relief fund functioned last year has put many municipalities on the verge of bankruptcy. This was an experiment, and the government has improved, although not completeley, the administration of this fund. They are not imposing the same harsh conditions upon the municipalities as were imposed last year; and because of that I am not prepared to fully condemn the government.
The next two paragraphs of the amendment deal in a most virtuous manner with the violation of election pledges. I agree with my Liberal friends when they state that many foolish pledges were given by Conservative candidates and by the Prime Minister which have not been redeemed; but if the leader of the opposition will go back to the first days of the special session, he will remember that when he warned the Prime Minister that he and his friends would look to the government to keep its pledges, I strongly protested. I said:	For heaven's
sake and the country's sake, we must prevent them from keeping their pledges! Had this government endeavoured to redeem all the pledges made by its candidates during the elections, Canada would be bankrupt.
The Prime Minister delivered last night one of the most eloquent and interesting speeches I have heard in my political life. He said that in spite of all theories he had a primary responsibility in dealing with the financial situation, and that was to save the credit of Canada. He stated in effect, that it would be better to be, what we term in French slang a "blagueur" than to ruin the country.
After forty years of parliamentary experience and some reading of parliamentary history of England, the United States and France, I have come to the somewhat cynical conclusion that all parties live in glass houses and should be very careful in the expression of indignation at their opponents for having broken pledges. I remember the elections of 1896 and the pledges given in Quebec by the Liberal party that they would restore the
Catholic schools in Manitoba. Pledges were given in the past by the Conservative party that they would never impose conscription during the war. I remember the pledges of the Liberal party that the moment they came into power they would eradicate the last vestige of protection. Yet the wind blowing from the south, the north, the east and the west has carried all these pledges into the deepest abyss of political oblivion. Could not, from the depths of that abyss, come the faint vapour of indulgence and political forgiveness to all parties?
The Liberals are not entitled to bring their opponents to task for this reason. The time may come when they will endeavour to prove to the people of Canada that their opponents are unworthy of the confidence reposed in them; and it may be that I, even in my old age, will put up a fight with them in an endeavour to convince the people of Quebec of that fact. But now, in dealing with this acute problem. I say, speaking with friendly candour, that my Liberal friends have been very ill advised in their present course.
The last paragraph, the one for which I would have been prepared to vote, reads:
That in the opinion of this house the provision of employment for our people is the most pressing problem before the present government, and immediate measures effectively to relieve the serious unemployment situation should be presented to parliament by the government without further delay.
Had the amendment contained only this paragraph it might have been accepted by the government. It may be said that being an amendment to the motion to go into supply, it would have been a vote of want of confidence in the government. I take issue with that view. Different governments, both in Canada and in England, have accepted amendments to the motion to go into supply when the amendment moved has been simply a suggestion of a policy which the government felt it could undertake. My mind goes back to 1901, when the Liberal government accepted a motion of this nature moved by Mr. Russell, then representing Hants, and now a retired justice. This amendment dealt with preferential tariffs, and the then Minister of Finance, the late Mr. Fielding, accepted it as being a suggestion of policy which the government was prepared to put into effect.
If the opposition had contented itself with pressing upon the government the necessity of adopting some practical method to relieve unemployment, and if the Prime Minister had stood up and accepted the suggestion in the same broad spirit, I think the country would have been better off, both morally and
Unemployment-Mr. Bourassa

politically, than it is at the present time, or than it will be after this amendment is voted down.
I am not going to vote against this amendment merely because it will be voted down; my past record is there to be seen. I have enough, I will not say of Irish blood but of Irish spirit in me, to induce me generally to be against rather than for the government. However, there is a limit to opposition; and as far as I am concerned, prepared as I am to criticize the government upon many of its acts of administration, prepared as I am to denounce the government at the next general elections should they not make more efforts to redeem those of their pledges which are capable of redemption and which would be for the benefit of the country, I am not prepared at this juncture, while we are still in the midst of a crisis, to vote for a motion of want of confidence which smacks so much of the party spirit as does the one now before the house.
Mr. E. C. ST-PERE (Hochelaga) (Translation) : Mr. Speaker, the question of unemployment is to-day of world-wide interest. It is known that the number of unemployed has actually reached 20,000,000 and the consequences of such a state we are told by certain economists have not yet been all felt. The outlook is really serious and of a nature to disturb the economic equilibrium and social order.
The motion of the hon. member for Kenora (Mr. Heenan) is of interest to workers. It will bring home facts that will elucidate the situation by showing them unemployment under its double aspect, international and national.
At the last session of the international conference held at Geneva, from May 8 to June 18 last, Mr. Albert Thomas, the director of the International Labour Bureau, made the following statement when he presented his report, and the workers of the city of Montreal as well as those throughout Canada will certainly be the gainers by closely reading the contents of this report:
Mr. Albert Thomas first pointed out the extent of the crisis which has deprived of work
20,000,000 people throughout the world, its serious side and persistence. Indeed, the crisis persists. There might have been a question, before the International Labour Conference could take up the subject, whether the situation might not have righted itself. Alas! no.
Recent statistics point out, it is true, that in some countries a slight improvement has taken place. However, it does not go beyond the seasonal fluctuation. In other parts, notwithstanding the seasonal influence, the crisis remains on the same level and at times even is worse. Notwithstanding Charles Gide's con-[Mr. Bourassa.l
tentions, this crisis is actually a fact. It not only exists in the minds of people who have been seized with a contagious fright. While the psychological element may play an important part, it is not the sole determining factor. The sufferings of the working masses deprived of work are truly a real tragedy which one cannot despise. In a word, the crisis has taken an international character. No doubt there are national crises, which have assumed specific features, such as the American, British and German crises. . . . But the depression is no less worldwide. Each country has its own troubles, but there is also a kind of universal depression which has spread everywhere and aggravates the troubles of all. Hence the necessity of an international remedy and the question which naturally presents itself is this: what is the International Labour Organization doing in the grip of such a crisis? What can it do?
Whatever may he the initiative it takes, Mr. Albert Thomas harbours no illusion on the dangers with which it is confronted. On the one hand, there is the appeal of those who demand immediately efficacious remedies: there is also the appealing confidence of labour centres, which expect almost salvation from the International Labour Organization and are tempted to ask more than it can give. On the other hand, there are those who remind us that the powers of the organization is limited, those who ridicule the long drawn out procedures of meetings, commissions, considerations and deliberations. . . . But is there in international life some means of evolving solutions by cooperative effort other than meetings to deliberate and forming commissions and conferences or in a general assembly? "We shall be compelled to have recourse to our system," states Mr. Albert Thomas. "After all, if we thoroughly organize our forces, perhaps, with such a system shall we make some headway in the present crisis.
However, the director specially points out that in such matters there cannot possibly exist an unique remedy. There is a whole series of solutions and remedies that should be classified, weighed and seriated: there exists no such thing as "the solution."
My intention in the present circumstances, like that of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), is not to consider the unemployment situation, as it appears to-day, by restricting it to my constituency and commenting on it solely for political purposes. However, it is a well known fact, namely, that at the last session of the Liberal regime, our leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), now the leader of the opposition, clearly explained that unemployment as it existed in Canada was simply the result of international conditions. He stated on many occasions that no special solution could be found to this problem which interests, among others, that class of workers to which appeal demagogues, fluent speakers but nevertheless devoid of sense, and who, in every constituency, endeavour at times to stir up trouble as between the classes. I represent, sir, one of these constituencies and in this I differ from my hon. friend from Labelle. The working classes in my electoral division satis-

Unemployment-Mr. St. Pere
fied that the present government would find work for them, relying on the assertions put forth by our opponents that the problem was purely a national one, that we were not suffering from a crisis entirely international in character, but from an endemic crisis, voted to some extent against me; the policy of the government that I supported was approved by my constituency but a large number of the electorate deemed this criticism well grounded and believed the contentions of our friends opposite to be sound.
Let us examine the program set forth then by our opponents to prove to the country that the unemployment question was only a national one. Let us probe into the arguments they put forth at the time, and let us ponder whether the policy advocated by them, counter to all reports submitted to the League of Nations and the International Labour Bureau, at Geneva, were not contradictory to the findings of these various commissions. This government, no more than the former government, must take it for granted that the findings of the commissions organized at Geneva under the aegis and protection of the League of Nations should be set aside by all nations. What do we find in the reports of these various commissions? All without exception maintain that if the tariff walls erected at present in all countries were to disappear the unemployment crisis would be half solved. If we are to reject, sir, the findings of these commissions, let us wipe out from our estimates the amounts that we yearly vote to have Canada represented at the League of Nations.
Viewing the matter in the same light as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) does, when he asks that under the present emergency, both political parties join their forces to solve the problem, I am willing to agree with him, providing that we agree with the findings which the various countries represented at every sitting of the commissions of the League of Nations have arrived at.
We are told that these are remedies which will improve the situation. They are to be found in social and unemployment insurances, etc. However, to better acquaint the labouring classes throughout Canada and those kind people who send me to Ottawa to represent them at each election, I shall explain to them the situation as it truly exists; for it is more than ever time to cease or to use the expression in vogue in the province of Quebec "to humbug" (emplir) the working classes of Quebec and Canada as a whole. The following is what Mr. Albert Thomas says in his report:
The director does not wish to enter into vague discussions as to whether unemployment insurance is liable to foster unemployment or whether, on the contrary, it can attenuate this scourge by maintaining the power of consumption of workingmen's families deprived of work.
However, he points out two striking facts, one quoted by Mr. Lawson, a delegate of the British government, the other by Doctor Brauns, a delegate of the German government. One always refers to these labour masses condemned for years past to unemployment, and the great demoralization which affects thousands, hundreds of thousands, even millions of people. It is important to bear in mind, as Mr. Lawson has pointed out, that, among the 12,000,000 people insured against unemployment in England, 35 per cent men and 48 per cent women -that is, on the one hand, more than a third, and, on the other, one-half-have never received any insurance indemnity. It is equally important also to be reminded of the figures given by Doctor Brauns: there are in Germany
5.000,000 unemployed, 17,000,000 are insured, however, two-thirds of the unemployed receiving insurance indemnity find work before completely exhausting their rights to insurance money.
It is but right therefore to remember that notwithstanding all criticisms-because unemployment insurance is indispensable for the future welfare of industry and for both the political and social stability of national organizations-there were, in 1919. about 4,000,000 people insured against unemployment and today. there are nearly 43,000,000 throughout the world."
My views, sir, with regard to social insurances are founded on principles which are dear to Christian democrats. I am in favour of all those social laws, such as unemployment insurance, etc., but on one condition, that they be explained to our people under their true light, that our people be not led to believe in a government's paternal solicitude, but that they be impressed with the fact, as I was, in Quebec, during the general election, that not a single worker, in any country whatsoever where these social laws are enforced, is dispensed with paying, together with the government and the employer, his quota to the unemployment fund. Whatever may be thought or said, we are, to-day, living in Canada under the dole syktem. The dole, as formerly understood in England, was an unemployment insurance based on a tripartite contribution, namely by the employer, the employee and the government. An attempt was made, at the last election, to make people believe that the Dominion government would burden itself with all these social laws and thus relieve the distress of our people during times of unemployment without any contribution on their part.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
No, no, may
I ask a question? Do you contend that the Conservative party, during the 1930 election, advocated a non-contributory unemployment insurance?
Finance Act-Mr. Spencer

Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	My opponent in my own constituency pledged himself to do anything except what had common sense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Your opponent was not the whole Conservative party; i refer to the Conservative parity's program.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	Let us now
examine the work carried out to relieve unemployment. Work given to the unemployed is a relief to the situation. I notice that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau), seems to cast an inquiring glance towards me, may I ask him, as head of an important legal office in Montreal, constantly dealing with contractors and workmen, whether there exists in his city a contractor who can state that more than 35 or 40 per cent of the money voted for work in connection with unemployment went directly to the unemployed? The greater part of that money was used to pay off expropriations or was expended in the construction of tunnels, etc., in the way of material. I may be told that the material which enters into these constructions affords work to a class of workers. I do not deny the fact that some workers benefit by such work.
Since parliament has now undertaken to settle this unemployment question, what are the best means to attain this end, if not to face the problem squarely outside all political considerations? The intervention of Providence in the present problem has often been mentioned; I am in earnest when I state that I believe in the intervention of Providence and, quoting the words of a free-thinker, Clemenceau, the distinguished French statesman, who said some time previous to his death: "If Christians truly practised their christianism, there would be no social problem." I shall go one step further than him and say that if we had always lived up to our Christian principles, there would never have been an economic question.
The problem, sir, which at present interests us-with this I shall close my remarks-is of the utmost importance. The duty of the Canadian government under the present circumstances, is to legislate in the interest of all. Considerations of a private order or personal feelings should not be taken into account. Let us legislate in the best interest of all, and especially, let us not forget to particularly look after the weak and humble, for, as Lacordaire one day said: Between the rich and the poor, between the strong and the weak, it is liberty which oppresses and the law which sets free.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF JUSTICE
subtopic: FINANCE ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Mr. H. E. SPENCER (Battle River) moved the second reading of Bill No. 23, to amend the Finance Act.
He said:	The bill that I am proposing to
the house asks for a certain amendment to be made to the Finance Act. The act as it now stands enables the banks and certain of the savings banks to take various securities to the treasury board and obtain, in return, an issue of dominion notes. This privilege, however, is not given to the provincial governments, although I find that two of the various classes of securities that may be taken to the treasury board and exchanged are treasury bills and provincial bonds. On the other hand, the banks of this country, which are private institutions, can take these same provincial bonds to the treasury board and secure an issue of dominion notes for a certain small charge. But the same right is denied to the provincial governments.
To-day we find that some of the provinces of Canada are having a certain amount of difficulty in financing. There are only two ways of getting money. One is by borrowing (a) through an issue of bonds or (b) through the banks; the other is by taxation. Certain of the provinces find themselves in such a position that they cannot issue any more bonds-not because they are bankrupt; we heard from the Prime Minister only last night, that some of the provinces are in very good shape indeed so far as their assets are concerned, but they have not been able to sell bonds. On the other hand, in some cases the banks, for reasons best known to themselves, have set a limit on the amount of overdraft which they will allow the provinces to make. Taxes on account of low commodity prices have been coming in very slowly indeed, so slowly that some of the provincial governments are unable to meet their indebtedness coming due. Some of the provinces are consequently in a very awkward position. I know full well that the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance will tell this house that the federal government has already come to the aid of the provinces in their need. That is all very well. Probably the Dominion government has had to come to the help of the provinces for the simple reason that it preferred to see them carry on

Finance Act-Mr. Rhodes
rather than default, but personally I do not like to see any provincial government put in the position of having to take second place to a private corporation such as our banks are.
The purpose of the amendment is simple It asks that the words "and to any province of Canada" be added to the act, so as to give to the provinces exactly the same right as the banks now enjoy in taking various securities to the treasury board with which to secure an issue of Dominion notes.
I well remember, Mr. Speaker, that when various banking questions were being discussed before the banking and commerce committee in 1928 the then Deputy Minister of Finance was asked by a member of the committee if it was true that the banks could take dominion bonds to the treasury board and get an issue of dominion notes under the Finance Act, and he replied:	Yes, it was. Then he
was asked:	If a private corporation like a
bank can take dominion bonds to the treasury board and get an issue of dominion notes under the Finance Act, why should not the Dominion government itself take the same dominion bonds to the same treasury board and get the same service? The deputy minister answered in this way: "Oh," he said, "that would be bad banking." I agree that that would be bad banking so far as the banks are concerned, because it would probably have some effect upon their profits. Then the deputy minister was asked: But why would it be bad banking? The only answer that he made at the time was: "Oh well, if I did that the Finance minister would fire me." So no real answer was given to the question.
In this bill, Mr. Speaker, I am simply asking that the same privilege shall be given to the provincial governments as is now given to the banks under the Finance Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
This bill, I submit, is so highly
objectionable in principle, if I may say so in all deference to my hon. friend who has moved its second reading (Mr. Spencer), as to border upon the realm of the fantastic.
The hon. member has referred to the fact that the provinces have found difficulty in financing and in selling their bonds. Speaking as one who has had some contact with provincial financing, let me say to my hon. friend that that may be a good thing; because in the past it has been perhaps a little too easy for the provinces to sell their securities. But that is merely by the way.
My hon. friend must realize that the provisions of the Finance Act were designed solely with a view to financial transactions 41761-44
as carried on by the banks. In large measure the Finance Act has taken the place in this country of the federal reserve bank in the United States. Its object was to make for an elasticity of currency from day to day as the needs require, but the very basis of the act was that the currency should be liquid. Now, if my hon. friend means that the provinces should come to the Dominion, and incidentally, I may add, make the dominion their banker, what does he suggest they should come to the Dominion government for? For the purpose of getting funds to be used in their current day to day transactions? If so, bear in mind that the revenues of the provinces must be derived from taxation, and the provinces should live within their income as provided by the taxation levied respectively by them. If any province is embarrassed in anticipating from day to day the receipt of taxation, that is a banking transaction which can be taken care of by the banks without any difficulty. But I submit, sir, that if the purpose of the provinces in coming to the treasury board should be to secure funds for the purpose of locking them up in capital expenditure, they would be doing something which is directly contrary to the underlying principle of the Finance Act and which is therefore doubly objectionable.

Quite so. However, I have known corporations, municipal and otherwise, to borrow for a year; and what if they cannot pay at the end of that period? It must be borne in mind that in addition to the security which 'the banks provide by virtue of the terms of the Finance Aot, there is a security which could not be given by the provinces themselves. That is provided by section 12 of the Finance Act, which not only gives the dominion the security of the lodged documents but in addition makes the following provision:
All advances of dominion notes made under this part shall be deemed to be an amount due by the bank to the government of Canada and shall be a second charge upon the assets of the bank, payment of a bank's own notes, issued by the bank, in circulation, being the first charge.
In other words, in addition to the security of the documents lodged by virtue of .the Finance Act there is the security of the assets of the bank, save only the bank's own notes in circulation.
If the proposal of the hon. member were sound, that is, if it were open to the province*

Finance Act-Mr. Rhodes

to avail themselves of the provisions of the Finance Act and to that extent make the dominion the banker for the provinces-which, I Submit, should not be-why should not the same principle extend to municipalities, cities and towns which would be in a position to lodge precisely .the same type of security? Furthermore, there is one very grave objection to the extent to which, if this bill became law, we would expand the borrowings under the Finance Act and to that extent indulge in a practice of inflation which .undoubtedly would have a very adverse effect upon the value of dominion notes.
Apart altogether from the objections I have offered to the suggestion of my hon. friend I raise the further point that consideration should not be given to this matter until a time during the next year when the Bank Act will come under review. So highly objectionable is this bill in principle that the mere fact of the house giving it second reading, and referring it to the banking and commerce committee would have an adverse effect upon the security of dominion finances. From every point of view I submit the bill is objectionable and should1 not .be read a second time. I hope hon. members will concur in that view.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the amendment before the house at the moment relates to problems of unemployment as they exist in Canada, and in particular to the measures the government of the day, since coming into office, have brought forward to deal with these problems. I do not think I exaggerate when I say that unemployment in Canada has become a national emergency, and that with respect thereto, the country is confronted with the greatest problem with which it has been faced since the time of the great war. The problem is not one of to-day alone; it has been continuous since the year 1930. Instead of conditions improving, they have become, despite the words of the Governor General's address, continually worse rather than better.
The amendment now before us recites some of the definite promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) during the election campaign of 1930, to the effect that he would end unemployment, and that, if returned to power, he, his government, or the majority behind him in parliament-in fact, he named all three-would see to it that work was provided for all who wished to work. "Work, not doles" were .the words he used1. It has been thought advisable to insert in the amendment some of those very definite promises. They are only examples, but they are sufficient to indicate the grounds upon which my right hon. friend made his appeal to the country, and, I think I am right in saying, the grounds upon which he was returned to office.
The amendment states that the measures the government has introduced are wholly inadequate and ineffective to deal with the problem of unemployment. I do not think I need cite conditions to verify the truth of that statement; instead of becoming better, conditions, as we all know, have continued to grow worse. Had the measures introduced been at all adequate or equal to the situation, there would have been a very great improvement. Indeed, at the time of introducing one of his measures during the special session, the Prime Minister drew attention to the fact that at that time there were about 150,000 unemployed, and stated further that, if the measures then introduced by the government operated

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
as the government hoped and believed they would, the numbers of unemployed would considerably diminish. Instead of diminishing, however, the figures have run up to 500,000 or
550,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Yes, that they were worse than anything we have ever known -and that, despite the measures introduced by his government to improve conditions. The amendment states that, ini the circumstances, it is important there should be other measures introduced to relieve the situation, and, even at this late date, that the government should bring forward something adequate and effective.
If it is necessary for me to refer to the past, it is because conditions as we have them to-day have grown out of the past, and largely out of the policies which have been introduced to meet them. I am not for any reasons of political partisanship going to refer to conditions as they existed at the time of the general election, and the respective attitudes of political parties at that time. My purpose in referring to conditions then existing is to explain to this House of Commons and to the people of Canada the respective points of view from which the problems then existing were faced by the political parties who were obliged to state their policies to the country, and to enable hon. members and the Canadian people to judge whether, even at this late date, policies which were advocated by hon. members who are now on this side would not have been more effective to deal with conditions as they have since existed
than those which, during the past two years, nave been put into force by hon. gentlemen opposite.
First of all, may I make it clear that the Prime Minister and the government have had a perfectly free hand to deal with this problem of unemployment. I do not think any hon. gentleman opposite will say for one moment that the Prime Minister and his government have not been afforded every facility a government could be afforded by parliament in dealing with this great problem. When the elections were over, one of their most important members, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce was defeated. He was permitted to be returned without opposition at a byelection. My right hon. friend desired to strengthen his cabinet by adding to it the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), who, at the general election had not been a candidate. He was not opposed in the byelection necessary to that end; he was allowed to take his seat without opposition. There was not a voice raised in criticism of the government when the special session of parliament was called; the ministry were free to bring in any measures they wished, and, the session having been called to deal with unemployment, the house took a very generous attitude towards the measures then introduced.
I am going to say a word about those measures in a few moments, to indicate whether or not what was said at the time, not by way of mere party criticism, but by way of substantial and constructive comment, has since been borne out by the facts. At the moment, I desire to make it clear that, notwithstanding the session was called to deal with unemployment, and that we were confronted with legislation with respect to the tariff more extensive than any legislation introduced in this parliament in any previous ten years, the government were allowed to put that legislation on the statute books practically without opposition. They were given equal freedom in the matter of the amount of money which they wished to have in order to deal with the situation.
Then the Imperial conference coming on was an important factor, the Prime Minister himself having stated in Toronto that on the success of that conference would depend in part the solution of the problem of unemployment. We offered no opposition to any attitude which he might take at the conference, and, indeed even when at the conference he took an attitude which we regarded as impossible and very wrong, no comment was made, except to have it clearly understood
692	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
that the attitude of the Prime Minister did not represent the point of view of Canada as a whole.
After the Imperial conference was over and before the next session of parliament came on, the ministry again were given a free hand; there was no carping criticism in the country, no criticism from the opposition, or from any grouip. Everyone recognized that the situation was serious, and the ministry were given a perfectly free hand. Last session again the government had an opportunity to bring forward whatever measures they wished, and I would point out that once more they were accorded every facility, but, as we well know, this [DOT] House of Commons was scarcely given an opportunity during that session to discuss the question of unemployment. The only measure respecting unemployment which the government introduced was not brought down until the very end of the session. It was the last item on the order paper during the last week of the session, with the exception of the two orders relating to the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means. If, therefore, the measures which have been introduced have not been effective, it cannot be said that this has been due to any opposition or obstruction which has been offered to the administration; it is wholly due to the administration itself.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I make clear that this is the third session of this parliament. We are here, for the third time since the present government came into power, to deal with a question which we were told would be settled immediately after the general election. As I have already said, I think it will be generally admitted that the question not only has not been settled, but that it presents a greater problem to the people of Canada to-day than it ever has before, a problem that is growing in seriousness week by week and month by month. No one will venture to say how grave is the existing national emergency. As a matter of fact, there are many of us in this House of Commons today who are very silent in reference to some of the conditions throughout this Dominion, as we have reason to know them to be, simply because we do not wish to create a state of alarm in the minds of the people, and also because we do not wish to embarrass the government in any way in dealing with a very difficult situation. I shall briefly review the measures which the government have taken to deal with this problem, to see how far they have gone in helping to meet the situation.
Mackenzie King.]
May I say that the ministry to-day, as I understand it, do not seek to contend that the problem has been settled, or that they have been able to deal with the situation. The Prime Minister will not say that he has fulfilled his promises. Indeed, the ministry is now stating that, had the conditions through which we are now passing, and through which we have been passing for the last year or two, been like previous industrial depressions, the measures which have been introduced would have been equal to the situation. They are saying that no one could have foreseen the problem which was ahead, and that for this reason, the government ought to be excused for being unable to meet it. May I recall, Mr. Speaker, that in the summer of 1930, and, indeed, in the spring of 1930, when this house was in session and the Liberal government had the responsibility of introducing measures in parliament to meet the then existing and the threatened situation, we pointed out that a certain economic situation had developed, as a result of changes in tariff on the other side of the line, which would necessitate our finding new markets within the British Empire to take the place of markets we were losing in the United States, and we framed our measures accordingly. When we came to the time of a general election, and there were evidences of depression, we made known to the electorate that the country was faced with a depression, though fortunately, at that time Canada was in a better position than other countries of the world. Above all else, what we sought to have the people of Canada understand was that this country, in common with other countries of the world, was facing an industrial depression, and that for that very reason, much as the government might wish to bring forward certain measures, and much as the government of the day might be tempted to make promises to the electorate as to what it might wish to do, the times would not justify anything of the kind.
That was the point of difference between my right hon. friend and myself in our appeals to the people in 1930 with respect to the approaching economic depression. To-day, the Prime Minister cannot shelter himself behind the statement that no one could foresee the depression that was coming on. If he had possessed a little wider knowledge of economic history, it would not have been difficult for him to look back over the century and see that at decennial periods for at least seventy or eighty years past, there have been these periods of depression, growing more serious as the world has become increasingly one. Had he possessed that

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
economic knowledge and applied it to the situation, he would have told the people of the country, as I told them, that we were face to face with a very serious depression, and that many things he might wish to do, if he were returned to power, he would not be able to do because of the inevitable depression. We took that position, and stated it very frankly to the people.
Instead of the leader of the Conservative party of that day taking, as I believe every member of his party expected he would take, a conservative attitude with regard to a very serious situation; instead of making it clear to the people of the country that he could not think of embarking upon vast expenditures at a time when economy was essential if people were to be spared vastly increased taxation; instead of making it plain that this was not a time when the federal parliament should begin to make anew fresh commitments in the nature of grants in aid to the provinces for all sorts of services in relation to technical education, in relation to old age pensions, in relation to highways and various other proposals;-instead of doing all or any of these things, he should have taken the position very firmly that, faced as we were with the approach of hard times, he could not make any such promises. Such was the attitude of the Liberal party. We made no promises except that we would endeavour to give to the problem of unemployment the best consideration which it could receive-and I will refer to that later on-and that we would seek to follow, in the future, policies which, in the past, had demonstrated their effectiveness in meeting an industrial situation such as then existed. We took and presented that view, and, the more firmly we held to it, the more lavish did hon. gentlemen opposite become in the promises which they made at random, and which, to secure the support of the electorate, they were prepared to make to any extent.
Now I say that we cannot afford lightly to dispose of promises made in that way. It is all very well for individuals, if they wish, to take a cynical attitude towards what is said at the time of a general election; but, if the outcome of conditions of this kind is not kept clearly in the public mind, there is going to be in the years to come no hope of saving the country from the effects of demagoguery as it will be carried on by political parties making their appeals to the people. An appeal to the people in a general election is a very serious matter, and too
much care cannot be taken, particularly by the leaders of political parties, in the pledges and promises they make.
Let me point out that there is a great difference between the promise that is made, the object that is to be attained, and the means by which it is proposed to fulfil the promise and attain the object. My right hon. friend will tell us, no doubt, that he promised that, if returned to power, he would increase the tariff; that if returned to power, he would make expenditures on highways and make grants in aid to the different provinces; that, if returned to power, he would embark on many other ventures involving expenditures of considerable amounts; and he will point to various things that the government is doing in these directions and say, " Am I not doing what I said I would do towards fulfilling the promises I made?" I say, sir, that he is not doing anything of the kind. His promise was that he would end unemployment; that was the promise he made to labour. His promise was that he would give, not doles, but work to everyone who wished to work. To the farmers of the country he said, "I will give you markets"; that was the appeal made to that section of the community. The means to that end were quite a different thing. What, were the means he said he would take ta that end? He said: In order to secure work for you, I am going to increase the tariff* I am going to introduce a protectionist regime in Canada; I am going to do more than that: I am going to spend very large sums of public money. These are to be the means by which I shall attain the end I have in view. When my right hon. friend made those statements, we, who took a different point of view, drew the attention of the country to the fallacy involved in his contentions. We pointed out that, instead of raising the tariff to meet a situation such as we then faced, we should do all that it was possible to do to increase trade, particularly within the British Empire, and therein find the markets which had been lost elsewhere. We pointed out that, at a time like that, no government that had any sense of responsibility could think of embarking upon vast expenditures which would necessitate increased borrowings with consequent vast increase of taxation, at a time when the people were feeling the effects of depression. We asserted that point of view and opposed our policies to his; and to-day this house and the country must judge as to who was in the right and who was in the wrong in the attitude then taken.
The point which I wish to make perfectly clfear is this. When I said that the country

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
would hold my right lion, friend to his promises, I was referring to his promise to end unemployment and to secure markets. I was not referring .to the means to that end, for I had already said in public over and over again that the means which my right hon. friend was proposing were not such as would prove effective to meet a situation of that kind. May I point out why those of us who were of the Liberal, administration of the day took the attitude we did. It was not taken without real justification.
At the time we came into office in 1921, this country was in a very serious depression. In fact, Canada was suffering from the most serious industrial depression that, up to that time, it had ever known. We had to face that situation. Our government came into office on December 29, 1921. In the previous fiscal year, 1919-20, there had been a deficit of 192,000,000; in the year we came into office-we were in for but three of the twelve months of the fiscal year; nine months had expired before we assumed the reins of poweT [DOT]-in that year there was again a deficit, this time of $81,000,000. That is the situation with which we were then confronted-a period of recurring enormous deficits. The Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, took very strongly the view that, unless we found it possible to balance our budget, unless in some way we were able to make revenues and expenditures meet, the country would be faced with bankruptcy, and he pointed out that we must shape our policies in a manner which would avoid such a condition by increasing the trade of Canada. Did we go about it as my right hon. friend is doing? Did we start by cutting down the salaries of public servants? Did we take measures that tended to reduce the purchasing power of the people at a time when it was desirable that purchasing power should be as considerable as circumstances would justify? Did we put up the tariff to a point where it would render impossible the shipment of goods to and fro across the ocean, making it absolutely impossible to bring in commodities from other lands on the vessels which we hoped to send out laden with our own commodities to distant countries? Did we not rather take the position that the only thing that would help to meet the industrial situation was so to frame the tariff as to reduce the duties on the implements of production in the great basic industries in order that those industries might develop, and the people engaged in them might compete favourably in foreign markets, and that our farmers might find

markets in distant lands? Did we not, in regard to all those things that enter into the family budget, all the necessaries of life, seek again so to adjust the tariff as to make the cost of living as reasonable to the people as the circumstances of the time would permit us to make them? Did we not also, with regard to the expenditure of public moneys, take the view that it was a time to economize: and that, much as we should like to do many things that governments, if they have plenty of money might be justified in doing, yet we could not enter upon such undertakings, but for the time being must retrench along right and proper lines so as to help to make ends meet?
These were the views we took. And with what result? With 'the result that at the end of a year or two we had changed the deficits to which I have referred-deficits of $92,000,000 and $81,000,000-into surpluses; with the result that, while we were in office only eight and a half years, in seven of those years we had surpluses in place of deficits. More than that, did we not take the position that, while it might mean something in the way of increased taxation at the outset we would endeavour so to shape our policies that taxation would bear as lightly as possible on those least able to bear it; and also that the burden to be imposed on industry would be as light as possible, hoping that gradually, thereafter we should be able to reduce taxation year by year, along with a reduction in the public debt. Again, with what result? With the result that in seven out of our eight and a half years, we reduced the public debt and continued to reduce taxation at the same time; with the further result that a new spirit was put into the life of 'the people, a new spirit was put into the industry of the country, and the trade of Canada began to increase to bounds it had never known before.
In other words, our policies were framed primarily with a view to developing trade, because we knew that as trade develops so will prosperity come to the country, and that only as trade develops will it be possible to deal fundamentally with the great problem of unemployment. There may be those who are inclined to put forward one particular nostrum or another as a cure for depressed conditions. In times of depression there are all sorts of theories afloat, all kinds of remedies are proposed such as the making of paper serve the place of gold, and other easy methods of getting rid of difficult problems. The world is not confronted to-day with these problems for the first time; it has been facing economic problems ever since there has been an

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
economic system in existence, and it has been found that only those policies which make for the furtherance of trade and help to develop the great basic resources and primary industries of a country will furnish ultimate solution to the great problem of unemployment. That is why we take the view which we do with respect to what we regard as so essential at this time with respect to tariffs and in respect of some other matters as to which there are differences in policy between ourselves and hon. gentlemen opposite. It has become customary for some to say:	Why
fight over again these old battles of free trade and protection?-to use the extremes of the issue; why fight over and over again the battle of tariffs? Why fight that battle? I ask hon. members to mark my words when I say that, as long as they live, they will find, not only in this country but in every country where tariffs prevail, the question whether tariffs are serving the people or serving special interests will be the great battle on the economic front. It is because tariffs may be so framed as to further the ends of special privilege at the expense of the great body of the people that this question must be always foremost in the country.

If Your

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
In dealing with the problem of unemployment as it presented itself during the campaign, the Prime Minister took the position that, if he were returned to power, he would call immediately a special session of parliament to end unemployment. That was the reason the special session was called after the Prime Minister came into office-it was a special session to end unemployment. What was the position taken at that time by the Liberal party in regard to the attitude of my right hon. friend? It was that a special session of parliament was not necessary to effect the end he had in view, that if it was public money he wished to obtain, he could obtain what was needed by way of governer general's warrant for a limited time, having regard to the fact that an imperial conference was to be held at which the government was to be represented, and that obviously a session of parliament could not last for any length of time prior to that conference. We took the position that more important than a special session of parliament was a conference of those most familiar with the problems of employment and unemployment, a conference representative of those who could best contribute to the devising of the most effective means of dealing with unemployment. Before parliament dissolved, before we went to the country, we had placed in the supplementary estimates a vote for $10,000 to provide for the holding a conference which would bring together representatives of different economic interests to consider what steps should be taken to deal with the problem. I explained in this house before, and I will explain again what we had in view in that connection.
It was intended to bring together, as had been brought together on a previous occasion, representatives of employers' associations such as the manufacturers' association and other employers' associations; of the labour organizations, such as the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress and of other labour organizations; representatives of the municipalities, such as the Union of Canadian Municipalities, representatives of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which could speak for the great trading interests of the country; representatives of the provinces; representatives of the Red Cross, of the great transportation companies and other organizations who would be
696	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
in a position to consider methods of cooperation in furthering employment and make helpful suggestions as to what might be advisable in the way of further steps to deal with this question. When that conference had come together our thought had been, had we been returned to power, to appoint an unemployment relief commission which would deal with this great question on a national scale, a commission which would be removed altogether from party controversy, which would be responsible to parliament through the government of the day, and which if the occasion so necessitated, would deal with the unemployment situation as a phase of a great national emergency.
In taking the step which we had in mind, we were but following what had been found to be necessary at another time of great national emergency, namely, during the period of the war. At that time it was found that while the departments of the government were capable of dealing in a regular way with matters of routine, they were not so manned and organized, and did not possess the expert knowledge or ability, either through the ministers or through the personnel, as to be able to undertake the handling of a great emergency situation, and that something of a special character had to be created. There was the Imperial Munitions Board, which had to deal with the question of the supplying of munitions for the war; there was the food control board, which had to do with the control of food, and there was a purchasing commission which had to do with the purchasing of supplies of one kind and another. As we all know, these different organizations were supplementary to the departments of government and were necessary because those departments were not equipped to handle an emergency situation. We took the position that that would be the proper way to deal with a question of this character, and I intend to show as I proceed that at each session of this parliament we stressed that step as the one which should be taken to deal with existing conditions.
May I point out this fact: We had it in our power, before parliament dissolved and we went to the country, to ask this house to give us one million, ten millions or twenty millions of dollars to enable us to deal with the unemployment problem. We are being criticized to-day because we did not ask for these amounts; we are being told that we were not sufficiently conscious of the nature of the problem because we did not ask that a grant of the kind should be made and then go to the people and

say: We have this money and we are going to spend it in curing your ills and in seeing that everyone obtains employment. We could have done that; but had we done it, what would have been the criticism of my right hon. friend opposite. It would have been that, on the eve of an election, we had taken out of the public treasury a million dollars or many million dollars to bribe the electorate. We would have been told that action of the kind was a reason why we should incur defeat rather than why we should be returned to office. With the knowledge I have of what governed the actions of the cabinet of which I had the honour to be the head, I may say that on the eve of an election we were doubly careful to take no step which was capable of a construction of the kind. We were equally careful during the whole election, whether we were to encounter defeat or victory, not to make to the country a single promise which we had not every reason to believe we would be able to fulfil in letter and spirit if we were returned.
My right hon. friend got his special session. What happened at it? As we know, when the special session met, we were confronted with changes in the tariff more sweeping in extent and higher than anything which Canada had known in the whole of her previous history Those measures were put through practically under a form of closure, because my right hon. friend told us that, if we did not allow them to go through, he would not go to the conference, and everything as to the future of Canada's development depended on what was going to happen at that conference. So those measures were put through. When we are discussing the measures which the government has introduced to deal with the problem of unemployment, we cannot escape from considering those changes that were made in the tariff without rhyme or reason, without advice or counsel from any source, that were made to a degree wholly unwarranted, and that have brought criticism upon the administration even by many of its own manufacturing friends in whose special interests those changes were made. Those tariff changes have had more to do with the problem of unemployment being intensified to-day than any other single factor that can be mentioned.
How can the government say: You must not attribute conditions to the tariff, when they know by the way in which it has been raised, by the way in which it has been manipulated, by the way in which it has been changed from week to week and from day to day, the arbitrary way in which it has been dealt with, that there is no longer certainty

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
in the minds of aay manufacturer, distributor, consumer or producer as to what the tariff is to be a day or a week hence. Men will not invest their money, will not place orders anywhere, because they do not know what they are going to be faced with when they come to settle their accounts. The tariff measures that my right hon. friend has introduced constitute a great contributing factor to the situation as it is to-day and are responsible for unemployment reaching the extent it has.
If the tariff legislation of the government had been in the least successful, I imagine it would find itself reflected in the trade of the country. maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
May I interrupt the hon.
gentleman for one moment? Would he kindly tell the house just what the policy of his administration would have 'been to relieve the unemployment situation had he been returned to power? Now just tell the house what you would have done about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Yes, I will. If my hon. friend had been able to hear when I was speaking, he would have heard that already, because I made it quite clear. I stated first of all that we would have had an unemployment relief commission upon which there would have been representatives of the parties who are best informed to deal with these matters, and they would have been given a free hand to deal with them, save that they would be responsible to the government and through the government to parliament. I said also that, instead of putting up the tariffs to umpardonable heights, we would have so arranged the tariffs as to help promote trade rather than restrict it. Finally, I have said, and I come to that point now, that instead of seeking an appropriation leading to lavish waste of public moneys, we would have used judgment in what we would have asked this house to vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Not a five cent piece.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I say to my hon. friend that it would have been better for him if he had not had five cents to-night.
May I come to the measure dealing with unemployment as such which was introduced by the Prime Minister at the special session?
I want again to impress upon the house the fact that it is impossible to separate, from among the government measures dealing with the unemployment problem, those that relate to the^ tariff and those that relate to the expenditure of public money. I have dealt with the tariff. Let me deal now with the lavish expenditure of public money.
Instead of the measure dealing with unemployment relief 'being brought down the first of all measures at the special session, it was the last measure to be introduced. There was really very little time, no time at all, to discuss it. What was the nature of that measure?

I have a copy of it in my hand. It was simply an act for the granting of aid for the relief of unemployment by a grant of $20,000,000.
May I here point out wherein I think the government has got itself and this country into the deep water in which it is at the present time in the matter of public expenditure? This government at the special session asked the house to vote $20,000,000 for unemployment relief. Remember, the special session was held in September and the fiscal year ends on the 31st of March. It was not necessary at the special session to vote money other than for the period that parliament would not be in session, and, had the rules and practices which should prevail in parliament obtained at that time, the government would not have asked and would not have received from parliament more than sufficient to enable it to tide over the time between that special session and the time at which the regular session of parliament would be called. However, the government asked for that period the sum of $20,000,000. I say, Mr. Speaker, that that estimate was not framed with any regard to what had been done in the past, or to the proper way of meeting the situation. The Prime Minister took a figure that was purely arbitrary, without relation to what was actually needed, without relation to what had actually been expended in previous years for a similar purpose, and had parliament vote that vast sum of money. Having at the beginning asked parliament to vote that vast sum of money, a little later on the Prime Minister was forced to take steps which were still more extreme.
I have said that when we came into office in 1921 there was existing a very serious industrial depression. The year before, the Conservative government of the day laid down a policy with respect to unemployment relief, which policy was: that unemployment relief, in the first instance, was essentially a municipal matter; in the second place, it_ was a provincial matter; and it became a national matter only when the provinces represented to the dominion that they were unable to cape with the situation. The provinces had in 1920 represented to the Conservative government of the day that they were unable to deal with the situation and had asked for unemployment relief. An appropriation was granted by this house for the purpose of unemployment relief in aid of the provinces and municipalities.
When we came into power in 1921 we found that we had to avail ourselves of a similar course of cooperation with the provinces and municipalities in meeting what had become a national need, and we utilized sums
, 1932	699

voted and voted other sums to aid provinces and municipalities in unemployment relief. That was done for two or three years in succession. Whenever during the following years the situation grew sufficiently serious to warrant the step, a sum was voted for that purpose, but the amounts were safeguarded and restricted. Altogether, in the period of ten years from 1920 to 1930 inclusive, there was spent out of the federal treasury in aid to the provinces, to meet the unemployment situation of the dominion, a sum of less than $2,000,000-something under $1,900,000 in the whole ten years, including the period in which the Conservative administration had introduced the method of providing relief which as indicated was followed by the Liberal administration. During those whole ten years there was not a total of $2,000,000 spent out of the public treasury for unemployment relief purposes. Yet in the special session in 1930 the Prime Minister came and asked this house to vote $20,000,000 and secured that amount to meet the situation during that one short winter.
How much of this $20,000,000 did he use during the period up to the end of the then fiscal year? I think $4,000,000 was about all that was used. True enough, commitments were made, on into the spring and summer, of moneys that might still be spent, and in one way or another nearly $19,000,000 of that amount was used up. I submit, however, that if the Prime Minister had followed the example of asking this parliament to vote an appropriation only for the period up to the end of the fiscal year, and had come back for what he needed for the new fiscal year, we might have saved, not one or two million dollars, but anywhere from ten to fifteen million dollars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen may have their views, but that is mine. At any rate, it cannot be denied that during the previous ten years not as much as two million dollars altogether was spent from the federal treasury for unemployment relief, in comparison with the twenty million dollars which was requested at that one special session by the Prime Minister for less than as many months.
