speechtext: Well spent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Then, having
received this large sum of money from parliament, and having spent it-some hon. member suggests it was well spent

what happens? The Prime Minister comes back

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
to parliament and says, "I want an appropriation, not for $20,000,000, not for $50,000,000, not for $100,000,000, but I want this parliament to give me a blank cheque, to allow me to take all the money I wish, and to be perfectly free to spend it by direction of the Governor General in Council." He obtained that permission from parliament; that was the second measure introduced. I say, Mr. Speaker, instead of a measure of that kind helping to meet the industrial situation, it has made it infinitely worse. Where is there throughout the length and breadth of this dominion to-day a man or woman suffering want or privation who does not know the Prime Minister has a blank cheque from parliament for an unlimited amount, and that he has been given authority to fulfil his promise that "there shall be work for everyone who wishes to work-not doles." In those circumstances has there not been added an element of poignancy and bitterness to the distress of those suffering to-day through lack of employment and insufficiency of food? First of all, by raising fears in the minds of people in this country as to the extent of impending calamity when he asked for $20,000,000 to meet unemployment, when $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 at the very outside would have been sufficient for the time, the Prime Minister caused capital to conceal itself and its owners to refrain from seeking investments in many quarters. On the other hand, by raising false hopes and stating that anyone who wished to get work would have it where there was no chance of fulfilling any such undertaking, he helped to make conditions infinitely worse than they otherwise would have been.
The trouble with my right hon. friend is this,-and I make the statement to him in all kindness, because in his efforts I think he means to be sincere-he is a man of extremes; he is never satisfied with anything that is not extreme one way or another. If he deals with the tariff, he must raise it higher than anybody else has raised it. If it is a matter of hopes, they must be raised higher than hopes ever before have been raised; if fears, those fears must be greater than have been known heretofore. Through extreme action in one direction and another conditions have been made more unsettled than otherwise they would have been. I say that, first, by arousing the fears of the people throughout Canada as to the extent of threatened unemployment; and, then, by raising false hopes as to employment for all which he has been unable to fulfil; and, now, by going to the other extreme of cutting off salaries, reducing staffs and the like-proceeding from one extreme to the 
other-he has placed the country in its present unsettled condition under which no one will venture to make with any degree of confidence a substantial investment in anything.
What further do we find in regard to the measures of the last session? My right hon. friend was not content to follow the practice other governments have followed in times of emergency and stress, when requests have been made to vote moneys and trust parliament to do the right and necessary thing. He was determined to deal in his own way, to get the whole business of relief into his own hands, and out of the hands of parliament. The measure he brought in at the second session was not that parliament should vote a certain sum but that he should be given powers-when I say "he" I mean, of course, the governor in council-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: No, "he" is correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Well, of course, as we know, my right hon. friend is more or less the governor in council. I say when he asked and obtained power from parliament to deal with the relief he went much further than any other Prime Minister in Canada has ever gone. At the time of the great war, Sir Robert Borden repeatedly had occasion to come to parliament to have parliament vote millions of dollars to meet war expenditures, moneys necessary for the maintenance of the troops at the front, for the sending of men overseas and the bringing of men back. Did Sir Robert Borden ask parliament to give him a blank cheque?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
No, not at
all. Sir Robert Borden came to parliament, asked for a specific sum of money, and requested that the money should be voted by parliament for a specific purpose and for a specific time. On no occasion, so far as I can recall, did he get from parliament authority to spend money outside the fiscal year for which it was appropriated. Never did he think of coming to parliament and asking for a blank cheque, but always asked for specific sums. My right hon. friend knows that we on this side of the house pleaded with him not to ask for a blank cheque, not to ask for the right to have moneys out of which commitments could be made beyond the period of the fiscal year. We asked him to have regard for the traditions, usages and customs of parliament. But he would pay no heed to our suggestions, and, at the last minute of the session, brought in and pressed through his measure.

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
My right hon. friend has talked about cooperation between the parties. What opportunity has been given to hon. members in this house to cooperate with the Prime Minister and his colleagues?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Every opportunity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
What opportunity has his own following had to cooperate with him or to offer suggestions to him? The measure to which I referred and which was brought in at the end of the last session was the last measure on the order paper. It was not brought in until the last week of the session, and hon. members will recall conditions in this chamber at the end of July and the beginning of August when this measure was considered. The whole session went by without the introduction of any legislation to deal with unemployment. Then, when every member was nearly exhausted, when all were preparing to go home, the Prime Minister presented to parliament the demand for a blank cheque. Under a process which very nearly approached closure-because when a measure is presented so late in the session that term may well be applied-he obtained the right, not only to spend all the money he wished, but the authority by order in council to make new offences, to impose new penalties, to borrow money as well as to spend it, and to do whatever he wished with respect to anything which in his opinion related to a solution of the unemployment problem.
Those are the measures which up to the present time have been introduced by my right hon. friend. I think I have already made it clear that, instead of becoming better, conditions have gone from bad to worse. There is one further step, however, which he has indicated it is his intention to take, and is one which makes a consideration of this whole matter at this time so important. The present indication is the only hint he has given us of the step he intends to take to meet the present unemployment condition. What is it? It would seem that he means while parliament is in session, to perpetuate the legislation for which he asked to enable him to deal with the situation when parliament was not in session. That legislation, the bill of 1931 to which I have just referred, was a means to enable the government to deal with unemployment after parliament had prorogued and before another session came into being. On the order paper to-day, appears the following resolution:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of
Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
What does this mean? Chapter 58 is the act to which I have just referred. It means that notwithstanding that parliament is in session, notwithstanding that the people's representatives are here assembled for the express purpose of dealing with the great problems of the country and voting supplies in the regular way, the Prime Minister asks this parliament to give to the ministry while parliament is in session the power to do by order in council that which should be done only by act of this parliament and by supply voted in the regular manner. A more audacious or amazing piece of legislation never was introduced to a free assembly by any prime minister. This measure proposes that, while parliament is in session, actually assembled here with representatives from all parts of the country, hon. members shall forego, by the changing of a date in an act of parliament, their whole duty of dealing in the regular manner with the problem of unemployment in what my right hon. friend will tell us is another emergent situation. "We must meet this situation in the west at once; people are starving; people need this help." If we hesitate for a moment to pass the enactment we will be told that we are blocking aid and holding up the relief that is necessary. The Prime Minister comes along with this measure and by requesting an extension of its provisions from March to May asks us to allow him to have this blank cheque to use while parliament is in session, though his reason for fixing the date at which the act should expire was that he expected parliament would be in session at that time, and that parliament would deal with matters from then on in the regular way. Now he says, "Let me have the powers here conferred until the month of May." What will happen then? I think what we will find, if my right hon. friend has his way, is this:	If he can
avoid discussion, and get away from being obliged to bring down any policy with respect to unemployment relief until the month of May, when May comes along we will find this parliament will be adjourned until the fall; we will be told that my right hon. friend and his colleagues have to get ready for the Imperial economic conference, and will need the next two or three months for that. Then there will be no discussion on the relief of unemployment or on the methods by which the problem of unemployment is to be solved, and the unemployed will be left to take care of themselves. I may be wrong, but I believe
"02	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
that is the purpose underlying this legislation,-to get away from any discussion at this time by giving the ministry what it needs for the next couple of months. Then they will adjourn this house for months without any settled policy with regard to unemployment having been arrived at.
Now may I point out to the members of this house the seriousness of the situation. This is the only indication we have had at this session, of the policy of the government in dealing with unemployment, and what is it? It is a continuation of the thing which has made matters go from bad to worse up to the present time. That is the position. There is nothing new in the proposed legislation. The government confesses, by the bill it is proposing, its impotence to deal with the question of unemployment; its incapacity and its total incompetence to offer any kind of a solution to this problem. We know that this measure which it is proposed now to extend till May has been a failure; we know that things have gone from bad to worse under the two acts already passed. The ministry will have to offer this parliament and the country something more than is contained in this measure, before the country will be satisfied with regard to the way the government is meeting the unemployment problem.
It is perfectly clear, Mr. Speaker, that the government has no policy for dealing with this question of unemployment, other than the continued expenditure of large sums of public money in the way here indicated. Indeed, the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) the other evening was a pathetic exhibition-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
-of complete incapacity to deal with the most important of all existing labour problems. Read his speech and you will see that the greater part of it was devoted to quoting from solicited letters relating to some petty squabble with regard to patronage up in northern Ontario. Two-thirds of his speech was taken up along that line, yet hon. gentlemen talk about- others seeking to make political capital. What was there in the nature of a constructive suggestion in the speech of the Minister of Labour, the only expression of view we have had from the government? What was there? There was not one single suggestion of any course of action other than that the ministry would continue cooperating with the provinces and with the municipalities though, as is stated in this amendment, the government itself is evading the responsibility of this being treated as a

national issue by making what it does conditional upon what is done by the municipalities and the provinces. It was the Prime Minister himself who said that unemployment had become a national question. He made that statement throughout the campaign of 1930, but to-day he seeks to back away from that position, at a time when it is becoming more of a national question -than ever before.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in order that no -one may say that nothing in the nature of a practical suggestion has been made, from this side of the house, may I repeat again to-night a suggestion which I made on behalf of the Liberal apposition, both during the special session and at the regular session a year ago, as to w-hat should be done at this time to deal w-ith this question-what should have been done -then and what I believe should be done now. I -believe that this problem of unemployment is going to be with us not*only for several months yet but, I fear, for another year or two at the least. I believe, if this problem is to be met, it cannot be met in the manner in which the enactments up to the present have sought to meet it, but that something very different will have to be devised. There is no man or woman in -this House of Commons who can devise a plan -that is going to -meet the situation, but I do believe that throughout Canada there are those who, -because of their special knowledge and understanding of industrial conditions, could, if they were brought together and given authority, deal with the great problem of unemployment in a satisfactory manner, or at least a manner as satisfactory as can be expected.
I suggest to the ministry that immediate steps be taken to appoint an unemployment relief commission, or committee, or whatever you may like to na-me the body. Ask the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress to nominate to that body some person or persons in whom they have the greatest confidence; ask other leading labour organizations to do likewise; ask the manufacturers' and employers' associations to name one or two members also; ask the union of municipalities to name a, representative; ask .the Canadian Chamber of Commerce to name its representative; ask the provincial governments, if you like, to lame their representatives; ask the Red Cross, which has had to do with administering relief, to name its representative. Let us have a body of experts and allow them to make recommendations to this parliament of what in their opinion may be necessary in the way of enactments or appropriations. Let them effect the necessary cooperation between the dominion and the provinces and the munici-

Unemployment-Mr. Mackenzie King
palities. We will then have something to guide us and help us to meet the situation. The Minister of Labour himself and his department cannot cope with this situation- and I make that statement with all deference. Already we have witnessed one minister of labour break down completely under the burden; with his own lips the Prime Minister has told us that if there ever was one martyred in his endeavour to cope with a great problem, it was the former Minister of Labour. The preceding Minister of Labour had an experience in industrial problems which, with all due respect, the present Minister of Labour, with all his ability has not had. Is it to be assumed that what Senator Robertson was unable to do while in the position of Minister of Labour the present Minister of Labour is going to do? It is impossible to expect from the present minister and his department any advance upon what we have witnessed up to the present, and it is absolutely essential that the work of unemployment relief should be coordinated in a much more effective way than is the case at the present time.
Having given, some study to the question of methods of unemployment relief, as well as to other phases of the industrial problem, I may be permitted to recall one instance in particular of which I have personal knowledge where a great state, confronted with the problem of unemployment, adopted a course somewhat along the lines I have just been indicating. The method which was adopted contemplated a most effective form of cooperation between the state, and municipalities, organizations and individuals. I should like to indicate what form that cooperation would take in this country if a similar method were applied here. I would suggest that, wherever work is being done in a municipality, the agencies of that municipality should be employed in the first instance to the extent to which they are capable of being employed. Municipalities have those in charge of their road work and work of construction. Allow, or rather oblige the municipality itself to provide its overseers, its superintendents, its supervisors and so on; allow it to provide what may be necessary in the way of equipment, tools, supplies, and the like. Let that kind of thing be done by the municipality. It will feel its interest; it will use economy in regard to its own expenditures. Let municipalities do all that they can do, and, when they have done all that they can, let the provinces come in with their facilities and special agencies for supervising work, for contributing supplies and the like. So far as the dominion government is concerned, let it come in when it has had an opportunity of coordinating the work as between the municipalities and provinces, and contribute its money in such a way that it will be used exclusively to pay the labour that is employed, not one cent of it going for supplies or tools or equipment or superintendence or in payment to contractors engaged on relief work. If that step is taken, the unemployed will get the benefit of what this parliament is voting. In other words, there will be a check as between the municipalities and the provinces, and a check as between the provinces and the dominion. Each will be interested in seeing that it is free from exploitation at the expense of the other, and, if this dominion adopts the policy of granting its moneys for the payment of actual labour, none going to contractors, none going to pay for supplies or equipment or superintendence or anything of that sort, then we shall find that the money which this parliament is voting by millions to help unemployment will provide work for those who are unemployed at the present time.
I offer that as a practical suggestion and I do hope my right hon. friend will accept it, and that he and his government will give it consideration. I submit that, with the Imperial economic conference coming on, and with all the other problems he has to deal with, he and his government have moTe to cape with than they can possibly manage. I give them credit for trying to do their best in the very serious situation of the country to-day; I think they are trying to do their best. But, I submit, they themselves must see that the measures they have brought in, up to the present time, are not adequate to meet the situation; instead, they are only tending to aggravate it. Can they not begin to throw off their own shoulders some of the burdens that are dragging them down, and to trust to others who are in a very favourable position to deal with the problems, giving them a free hand for the purpose? The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) this afternoon spoke of partisanship and playing the partisan game. Surely there is nothing of partisanship m a suggestion such as I have offered; rather, it is a means of getting away from partisanship. And that is what I am seeking to do at -the moment; I a-m trying to induce the government to establish some representative body in which the country will have confidence.

It may be done here and there in connection with some of the relief of rural distress in Saskatchewan, but it is not being done in the province of Ontario. It is not being done in the province of Quebec; it is not 'being done in the maritime provinces; it is not being done in British Columbia. What I want done generally is the kind of thing that the hon. member says is being done with relation to one locality only, but not done by a partisan commission, if I might so say to my hon. friend. The government have 'to take the responsibility for the commission they appoint. If they are unwilling to leave to responsible bodies the naming of persons whom they are prepared to trust, that, of course, is their privilege; they may name their own commission. But I think the country will judge the government in their meeting of this great national emergency by the non-partisan character of the commission they appoint, and the qualifications of those who compose it.
We are not at this stage in a position even to discuss this question as intelligently as it should be discussed because we have not yet before us what the government has done under this very enactment which expires to-day. We have not yet received any statement from the government as to what has been done. And that brings me to the concluding part of my remarks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen say, "hear, hear." We shall see what they have to say when I finish what I am about to say at this moment.
What is the position to-day with respect to the government's policy for meeting unemployment? No word has come from the ministry since this third session of parliament has assembled. In the speech from the throne there is not a single word with respect to any policy for meeting the unemployment situation. The only statement made there is that conditions are improving, and that is not true. There has not been a word from the Minister of Labour or the Prime Minister in regard to any sort of proposal to deal with the question of unemployment. There was a discussion the other day with regard to expanding the scope of the industrial research council. A suggestion came in the form of a motion by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) that there should be appointed a body similar to the industrial and scientific research council to deal with social and economic questions.

When that measure was brought forward, I repeated this year a suggestion I made last year, that, if the government was not prepared to appoint a commission to deal with thi3 problem of unemployment it might at any rate appoint a few experts, under the powers given in the Industrial Research Act as it exists to-day, and allow them to work in cooperation with the government on the question of unemployment, much as the tariff board did in advising the late government on matters affecting the tariff. I suggested that it would be advisable to have some board of that character appointed. That suggestion I made last year, and the government turned a deaf ear to it. This year I have made it again, and, up to the present time, no recognition has been given it.
Has any committee of parliament been appointed to investigate this great problem of unemployment? How, may I ask, are we to measure the zeal of the government in these matters? My right hon. friend did not hesitate to put before everything else a matter of personal concern to himself and submit it as a subject of investigation by a committee of this house, even before His Excellency the Governor General had been thanked for his speech; and to-day we have a committee of this parliament investigating certain matters that are peculiarly personal to the Prime Minister. Where is the parliamentary committee dealing with the question of unemployment? Where is the committee of the Commons appointed to consider this great problem of unemployment relief? Where has there been at this session a single word by the Prime Minister, who said in seeking office, "I will end unemployment; I will see that everyone has work"-where is the word from him about the distress and suffering throughout the country as a consequence of unemployment after he has been in office a year and a half? I say, no parliamentary committee has been appointed in connection with this matter, the greatest of all problems with which parliament has to deal. Not a word from the Prime Minister thus far this session.
And what have we had from the new Minister of Labour? Not a suggestion in the speech he has made; no suggestion of any policy. Finally, to come to the resolution itself, which is all we have had up to the present time even by way of indication of what is to be expected, I take it to signify an attempt to escape from any discussion of the problem of unemployment, if this is possible, until this session of parliament prorogues. Let me read it:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the Statutes of

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
When was this notice given? It was given just a week ago to-day; that, I believe, was when this notice was put on the order paper. Why was it not put there during the first days of the session? Why up to the present time have we not had a discussion of the question of unemployment? My right hon. friend is not slow in appreciating the significance of every move he makes; but what is the position to-day? Let me read the section which it is proposed to amend. My right hon. friend is proposing that we shall substitute for the word "March" the word "May", in the act passed at the last session of parliament. It is intended to amend, in this manner, this particularly section:
This act shall expire on the first day of March, 1932.
Well, this is the first day of March, and this act has expired or will expire at midnight to-night, so that what my right hon. friend is proposing is that we shall amend a statute that no longer exists. This is his contribution to the unemployed of the country. No suggestion in the speech from the throne, no committee of parliament to investigate the matter, no special committee to advise the ministry, no statement of policy from the Minister of Labour or -the Prime Minister-the only proposal made by the Prime Minister is to amend an extinct enactment, to amend a dead statute. That is what the right hon. gentleman offers in the name of his government to those who are suffering and who are in need. He knows as well as I know that that bill is as dead as Julius Ceasar; it expired last night. He knows that that statute is of no more value than the majority of those passed in the reign of Queen Anne; he knows it is as extinct as the dodo. He comes to this parliament and offers to those who are without employment and need relief the amendment of a statute which no longer exists! What will the unemployed of this country think, what will those who are suffering from need and privation think, of the solicitude of the Prime Minister for them in their present condition?
Listen to what he said when he was appealing for power. Speaking in Vancouver on June 18, 1930, the Prime Minister of to-day, then the leader of the Conservative party, referring to myself, said:
However blind he may be to your future and deaf to your present needs, surely he cannot stop his ears with smug complacence and selfesteem to the cry that carries across the nation -the cry of the destitute and hungry, the cry 41701-45
of mothers and fathers and little children who call to us as Christians and as Canadians to heal their pain.
"Who call to us as Christians," he says: may I remind the Prime Minister that the Pounder of Christendom itself used the words:
Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?
And also:
Or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent?
The women and children who are suffering in this country to-day have asked the Prime Minister for bread, they have asked him for work, but he has given them not even a stone or a serpent; he has given them an extinct enactment, he has given them a dead statute.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as it is probable that a vote will be taken on the amendment before the house, and since that amendment is regarded in parliamentary parlance as being a vote of want of confidence, and further since it involves a subject which is so important that it cannot be ignored, it becomes essential that the members of the group in this corner should express their view.
The opportunity presented by this amendment for a discussion of the vexed problem of unemployment is not as propitious as might have been desired. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), in 'his usual forceful eloquence, expressed the sentiments of the members in this corner when he decried the fact that this amendment had been offered in a political setting. It is very unfortunate that a question of such profound significance to the people of Canada should be brought into parliament in the manner in which this amendment presents it.
Undoubtedly we are all looking to the administration and to this parliament for a solution of the unemployment question, and as far as I am able to judge of the matter we will require to evolve a twofold policy. One policy will deal with the giving of sustenance to the people of Canada, the providing of support for those who have lost their means of livelihood because of a lack of work. That is the first task to be faced by the administration. The second policy should be designed to bring about an ultimate or fundamental reformation which will remove the economic cause of unemployment. The policy of providing work for unemployed rather than giving charity, was brought up at the last session of parliament, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has just stated. At that time it appeared to me to be the general opinion of this house that the policy of

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
providing work for the unemployed was more acceptable than that of the granting of doles. It seemed to be a plausible policy, and I think it was generally agreed that it was the best, but I am not so sure to-day that it was. I have visited some of the relief camps which have been established under the control of the administration and I found them to be very satisfactory. I refer, of course, to the camps established for the building of a highway in northern Ontario. The work was being engaged in by the workers with a good deal of zest, the places where they lived were clean, wholesome and comfortable, and the food provided of an excellent character. If all the unemployed in Canada could enjoy the same conditions I do not think there would be anj immediate cause for objection. However, I believe that such relief projects ultimately will have to be abandoned. I express that opinion reluctantly, but in view of all the circumstances I am afraid that that is what will happen. It is clear that no government has ever entered into any industry similar to that being carried on by private institutions, because to do so would mean that the government so doing would come into conflict with private property and the capitalistic system in general. The activities left to a government to undertake on behalf of the unemployed must be of a class usually undertaken by governments, and this is limited to a certain kind of so-called public works. The most popular kind of public work undertaken by governments in cases of unemployment in this country is that of building roads and highways, because private companies do not usually do that. What is the situation in that regard? We find in the first instance that governments must borrow the money with which to carry on that work, and at the present time such money will be borrowed at a very high rate of interest, thus paying to the bondholders not only the usual but even a higher interest rate than it is customary for them to collect. Next, the work on those highways is frequently given by way of contract, although this has not been done in the locality I visited. It is given in some instances in Alberta, I believe, under contract through the municipalities and the provincial government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Not in Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
That allows a profit for the contractor. Then the materials are purchased at prices which permit a profit to those who deal in the commodities required. That leaves the lowest figure of wages to 'be paid to the people for whom all the work was originally undertaken, and finally, to cap the climax, as we

sometimes say in popular iparlance, the government has to accept what might be about 60 per cent of the actual work value for the money that it has expended. That is to say, work undertaken on roads and highways in the winter time in this country is very difficult to perform economically and the result usually is that about 60 per cent of what would be done under suitable conditions would be given under the present circumstances. For those reasons I doubt whether the policy of the state providing work to meet an unemployment situation, which has became so serious as to be described by the leader of the opposition a few minutes ago as a national emergency, can be carried on. However, the government must pay the bill. Winter work, as I say, is not an economic proposition, with the result that the government has to pay a very high sum for a very low return, and in view of the present financial situation throughout the world, I doubt whether such a policy can be continued indefinitely. The government of this country, like the governments of other countries, will ultimately be forced to take what may not be the best course, 'but the cheapest course, and under the present circumstances the cheapest course in the last analysis is undoubtedly that of giving doles instead of trying to give work. I am not advocating giving doles; I do not think that is a cure of unemployment, but in view of the financial stringency through which we are passing, the government may be forced to take the cheapest course instead of the best. But in any case I would insist that the people in Canada who have no money or work and thus have no food, shall be fed, clothed and sheltered. To do that, the state must assume the responsibility and must pay the bill. It remains for us to discover the best method by which the state can render that assistance to that part of the population which requires it.
In regard to the other phase of the matter, namely, the ultimate policy, I do not regard this as being an opportune moment to express whatever opinion I may hold in that respect. As the leader of the opposition has pointed out, there is on the order paper a measure which will afford an opportunity for a discussion of that sort, and I have no doubt, before the session ends, the government will furnish-at least I hope it will-an opportunity of discussing this question under more favourable circumstances. But in passing I would say that reformation, fundamental and constructive in regard to the economic problem which causes unemployment, is imperative. That reformation must and will come either

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
by legislation or by revolution. If parliament wants to prevent the latter, it must see to it that it provides the former. We must provide legislation that will bring the reformation necessary if we are to (prevent disaster in other ways. Parliament and the government must not forget that if we are to avoid the difficulties which we sometimes fear will arise, we must dio something to prevent the necessity for such action being taken. There must be an approach fundamentally different from that made by any nation so far, and from an entirely different understanding of the problem.
In that regard I am constrained to make a reference to the speech which has just been so eloquently delivered by the leader of the opposition. With perhaps this corner in mind, he referred to the nostrums of one kind or another which are sometimes proposed as a cure for the economic ills of our time. I do not of course know that he referred to this corner, but it is probable that he did. I do not think that in that respect this corner has pinned its flag to any particular masthead, although it is true we have advocated a number of things which we believe have an economic bearing on the problem. But leaving that aside, the leader of the opposition says that the economic problem is the same to-day as it has been ever since the world had an economic system. If he really means that, he is announcing his incapacity to lead any modern nation in the circumstances now confronting it; for I challenge his view in that regard and say that never before in the world's history has there been a situation similar to the present one, and that no policy that has been satisfactory in the past can possibly be applied to the present day. It may be all very well for him to say that the lower tariff policy of the Liberal party is going to be good enough for all time. I do not believe that, neither do I believe that the high tariff policy of the Conservative party is going to be good enough for all time. In fact, I would say that neither has been good enough for any time, and I do not think either has a very serious bearing upon the economic problem of the present day.
If we are going to continue industry on the basis of competition for private profit, it is certain that we shall end in disaster. All efforts made to cope with the situation on that basis I regard as being foredoomed to failure. Sooner or later this parliament and country must make a definite decision on that matter. Until that decision is made I am not very much interested in any proposal, no matter what side of the house it comes *41761-45J
from, because I firmly believe that unemployment cannot be cured under the present economic system, and that the first step towards a cure is a definite decision by the government and parliament that a new system must be introduced. Shall we continue to nurse the aged and dying system while youth and hope die for lack of attention? That is the problem as I see it. The decision, as I say, must be made to reconstruct our economic life on a new basis and for purposes very different from those which obtain now. Until that decision is made, I repeat, I have not very much faith in the outcome of any proposal which has in view the ultimate ending of unemployment.
Meanwhile, may I point out that Canada's richest deposits of wealth are being wasted and worse than wasted. Canada's youth is her richest vein of gold. What opportunities have we provided for the armies of young men and women who are coming year by year into the industrial field demanding the right to live by labour? I ask that question of myself and I ask it of every hon. member in this house. Coming up for the year 1932 is an army of bright and intelligent young men and women of Canada. A similar army came up last year, and one the year before; another will come the year following, and they are faced with closed industrial doors; opportunity for expansion in life's affairs is denied them. What is parliament going to do this year in order to give these young people an opportunity? The nation which cannot find opportunity for its youth will die of premature senility, and it deserves the fate. While Canadian youth is faced with that disaster we squabble in this house for a solid two days over a matter of political prestige or advantage, without bringing forward a single constructive policy to solve the problem. That is the fact of the matter as I see it. I mention the plight of youth not to be rhetorical, but to bring home to this parliament more poignantly if possible than anything else could bring it home, the importance of the question now before us and of finding some solution for it before we leave to go back to our homes.
I come to the amendment which has been proposed. I have no doubt-at least I am not permitted to doubt-that the hon. member who moved this amendment (Mr. Heen-an) is sincere in his objective. But it is rather a remarkable thing that the late Minister of Labour should find nothing better to offer to the unemployed than a huge hash of the speeches of the Prime Minister for the last three years, and that is what he brings to this parliament as a solution of the unem-
Unemployment-Mr. Irvine

ployment problem. I shall not weary the house by reading what has been read already half a dozen times, in the last few years, has been placed on Hansard on different occasions and given to the country in various ways. I fail to see what significance it can have in relation to the unemployment problem other than a political one. I do not know if it is really the case, but certainly it appears to me that in the amendment the reference to a solution of the unemployment problem is more of a means than an end to be gained. Of course adoption of the motion involves the defeat of the administration, and it is distinctly political in its objective. We are not very much interested over in this corner in the life of this administration or any other, nor are we particularly interested in the hopes of the opposition to get over where the present administration now is. That question has never been a very serious one for members of the group over here. Nevertheless, we are forced to express an opinion and sometimes to vote on questions of this character, and we must indicate our position.
The amendment in itself, I say, is distinctly political in character. When we look at the amendment in the light of the statement of the leader of the opposition, that unemployment has become a national emergency; when we look upon unemployment as a national emergency and then look at the resolution which is proposed to meet that national emergency I really do not know what to say about the matter. It is beyond comment. So far as our group here is concerned, and I think I am speaking for the group in this regard, we are not going to vote for the amendment, because we regard it as purely a political amendment, but we say to the hon. gentleman who moved it and to the leader of the opposition that whenever they bring in a positive resolution that will bear upon the problem of unemployment we shall be more than glad to stand with them. But when it comes to a matter of this sort, to an amendment which has clearly but one objective and that the making of political capital out of this national emergency, we do not intend to sustain their desires with our votes. On the other hand, we do not feel disposed to vote against the amendment, for this reason:	We
do not think the government has solved the problem of unemployment any more than do the hon. gentlemen who have been proposing and supporting the amendment, and we are looking forward to a statement of policy by the government in this session of parliament on this Question. Therefore we would not like to indicate by our votes that we are

perfectly satisfied with all that the government has done in the matter. On the other hand, we are not hypercritical. We know that the problem has been difficult. We know that the government has done something. We know that they have kept people from starving. We are looking forward to a better policy. So, Mr. Speaker, this is one of those peculiar motions in respect to which we shall take shelter by not voting at all, neither for nor against, but rather await the proposal of the government, or a better proposal from the opposition, bearing on the problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I approach this very important subject of unemployment in a non-partisan spirit, and will rather seek to submit some constructive suggestions which might be of benefit in helping to relieve the unemployment situation, more particularly as it concerns the province of British Columbia.
In so far as the amendment condemns the government for world wide conditions which they could neither foresee nor prevent, I am not in sympathy with it. The amendment is on surer ground when it condemns the government for the extravagant promises on which it rode into office, promises made recklessly and apparently with very little regard to the possibilities, let alone the probabilities, of their being capable of fulfilment. Some responsibility perhaps attaches to the electorate who so readily and credulously swallowed statements and promises which an application of ordinary, common horse sense might have told them were obviously insincere, or at least, obviously impossible of fulfilment. However, as my desk-mate, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has said, that is a matter of eighteen months or two years ago, and no great advantage can be gained to-day, as we see it at any rate, by reproaching the government for the non-fulfilment of promises, the blame for which centres rather around the fact that they were made at all than that they are now found incapable of fulfilment.
The people, as the hon. member for Labelle says, are looking to us to give them some lead, if such can be done, to bring them out of this economic depression. I blamed the government for two actions in connection with their relief scheme of the last year. First, I blamed them because they did not grasp soon enough the seriousness of the situation. Hon. members in this corner of the house and myself repeatedly urged the government concerning the necessity for prompt and immediate action. Such action was not taken. Had it been taken perhaps we would not have

Unemployment-Mr. Neill
seen the spectacle in British Columbia of ill-clad men, in some oases under-nourished, attempting to build roads in the heavy winter rains or at times in eight or ten inches of snow. Such conditions certainly did not promote efficient work, and the health of the men employed must have been affected.
The second fault I found was that too much power was placed in the hands of the provinces. The federal government did not retain enough control of the large sums of money which were being spent and for which they were primarily responsible.
Apart from those two objections I believe the present government made a genuine effort to relieve unemployment last year, and the fact that the results have been so disastrous in British Columbia is, I think, much more the fault of the provincial government than the federal. We may compare the actions of the provincial and Dominion governments in this way:	The
Dominion government did a considerable amount of work on its own hook. That is to say, work done which was wholly dominion in scope and paid for by the federal government. For the most part very little waste took place in that work. In common with other members of the house I was asked to furnish a statement recommending the most necessary works in the district I represent, and I did as requested. I was very careful to include only those works absolutely necessary, and included only those which had been omitted in the ordinary estimates and which should have been provided for in the usual maintenance vote. While the government did not carry out all the works I recommended, as it should have done-they were all very necessary-still all the works they did carry out were amongst those included in my list. I am sure I must have had the support of the government engineers who knew that the works were necessary for the maintenance of those wharves, floats and the like for which the government were responsible.
Of course there was a certain amount of abuse. Two regulations made lby this government were largely ignored. One of them was to the effect that so far as practicable the men employed should be residents of the locality in which the work was being performed. In many 'cases that regulation was ignored. A second regulation stipulated that in no case was discrimination to be allowed or permitted through political affiliations. That also was not properly adhered to. Further, men were employed who were not registered, yet the local government had expressly arranged a system of registration and
had provided and insisted through public notices that no man who had not registered would after a certain date be employed on relief work. That regulation was not complied with. In many cases men were selected on the recommendation of local politicians seeking only personal advantage, and in some cases selections were made on the advice of some would-be kaiser who could not resist the opportunity of inflicting political revenge on persons who, or districts which, in his opinion had not voted properly. If time permitted I could, if challenged, give definite instances of breaches of these regulations.
As I have said, this political manoeuvering took place in British Columbia; it did not take place in Ottawa. I wish now to follow the example set by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) who a few nights ago gave credit to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) for fairness in the administration of his department. I also am pleased to bear witness to his fair-mindedness. In more than one instance when I found that work which should have been done perhaps two years ago, work recommended by government engineers, was being sidetracked for no reasons other than political antagonism, I communicated with the minister and he in turn took steps to see that the grievance was rectified. At the moment I have in mind a situation which (Obtained in Lasqueti Island where three small works were needed, and where the most important one, on account of political intrigue, was being neglected. I give credit to the minister for his attitude in connection with -that work and will take every opportunity to see that he, a Conservative Minister of Public Works in a Conservative government, gets credit for his action in that regard. Despite some defects I think I can say that for the most part the work was wholly necessary and done efficiently. There were one or two small instances where through political influence some man would be put in charge of a little job who barely knew at which end of a canthook to apply himself, and perhaps was not very willing to apply himself at either end. These were small matters, however, and on the whole, there could be very little complaint.
A very different tale must be told, however, when we consider the work done by provincial authorities in which the federal government was interested. I might explain that a large part of British Columbia, other than areas within city municipalities, is unorganized. In those parts the provincial government had full control of the way the money was spent or, probably I should say, misspent. There
Unemployment-Mr. Neill

was very little complaint of the way work was done in the cities. I do not know what custom prevails in the east, but in the west councils are elected on a non-political basis, and consequently there was no opportunity or temptation to play politics. But the cities themselves had grievances. Dealing with the province, the cities found great difficulty in getting their proposals accepted. I have a record of one city in my district which asked for $20,000, and after extensive negotiations they were told they would receive only $10,000. Accordingly they financed on that basis but were told long afterwards that they would receive only $7,000. When the figure was agreed to there would be further delay in receiving an O.K., and still further delay when moneys were to be paid.
Speaking on this subject the other day I said I believed that I would be acting in the best interests of British Columbia if I urged the government seriously to consider the appointment of a commissioner with very sweeping powers who could go to British Columbia and handle the situation very much as though that province were more or less in the hands of a receiver. I said also that a strong capable man was needed vested with wide powers. After the necessary time required for Hansard to reach the province of British Columbia there appeared in a Victoria newspaper-I shall not give the name of the newspaper so that the columnist will not receive the publicity he was no doubt seeking but to which he is not entitled-an article attacking the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and myself. They accused my hon. friend of asking for, and accused me of supporting, his request for a commission. The suggestion in the article was that the request for a commission bore with it an insinuation that there was something to investigate in connection with relief work. The words I used were a little more definite than the word "insinuate." I said, "the whole thing reeks with suggestion of graft and corruption." There is no insinuation about that. The article went on to say that I was animated bjr a desire to show that I was still the champion of the rights, liberties and interests of the common people. As a matter of fact, referring to the Hansard from which I have just quoted, I find the hon. member for Vancouver Centre did not use the word "commission" at all. He did say that he would like to see a full investigation. Nor did I ask for a commission; I asked for a commissioner, a very different request. So far as the third rate columnist of a second rate newspaper is concerned I am quite happy to accept the

position he wishes on me-in fact I am rather proud to be classed as the champion of the rights and privileges of the common people. I am glad he knew enough to say that I am the champion of the rights and privileges of the common people, although on that occasion the words I used were "the whole of British Columbia."
Then again, Hon. Mr. Bruhn, the Minister of Public Works, rushes into print and says:
Mr. Neill expressed his belief that the administration of unemployment funds should be placed in the hands of a strong minded official with strict power and authority from the Dominion government.
Then he goes on to say:
This_ is the first time that we have known Mr. Neill to advocate a dictatorship when dealing with the unemployed.
I did not use the word "dictator," but if I had I would not have been alone. Let me quote this sentence:
The provincial government very much requires the services of a financial dictator. . . .
That is from the Vancouver Province, the strongest Conservative paper in British Columbia. Further on they use this language:
. . . we should say that such a tangle as obtains to-day in the relief camp service is an extremely strong indictment of the present system of control.
Thus speaks the Conservative newspaper, which in many respects is very fair-minded. As I said, I did not use the word "dictator," though I do not know that its use would not have been justified. What I advocated was not a dictator but a man whom I might classify as a go-between, with the Dominion government on the one hand, who have the money and are willing to spend it for relief purposes, and on the other hand the unemployed people who need relief work, who are anxious for it and who are going hungry for lack of it, but who do not appear able to get it because of this government of inefficient misfits in Victoria. I wanted somebody with sufficient power and authority to exercise some check over those governing curiosities in Victoria who have been blocking the progress of unemployment relief, who have been a nuisance to the government in Ottawa, a reproach to their party friends in British Columbia, and a curse to the unemployed who sought relief.
I am not attacking the Conservative government of British Columbia as such, but if I should do so I would be in very good company. There are a lot of Conservatives, including members of the local legislature, who are very frank in expressing their views of the situation. Perhaps, with a little exaggera-

Unemployment-Mr. Neill
tion, I could best express the situation by saying there is no Conservative government in British Columbia to-day; it has ceased to be, though it still carries the name, perhaps in the same way a woman who has betrayed her husband will for a time shelter herself behind his name and protection. The rump cabinet of Victoria has betrayed the Conservative party, and not only the Conservative party but also that wider section of independent people, whose numbers are growing in British Columbia, who do not vote according to party lines but who vote for what they think is in the best interests of the province. At any rate the Conservatives, and no doubt many Liberals and Independents, did vote for the government, and the best elements of the Conservative party promulgated a platform to which they were pledged and which they were determined to carry into effect. They were pledged to greater efficiency, greater economy, tax reductions and non-patronage, but their cabinet has broken every one of those pledges in turn and now, in this last fiasco in connection with unemployment relief, they have broken them all at once. I reiterate what I said the other night; the local government has made a complete mess of the unemployment situation.

Dr. Tolmie, decent, honest man that he is, who I hope soon recovers from his indisposition, would be one of the first to admit that conditions are unsatisfactory. I know this was a very great nightmare to the previous Minister of Labour, and I believe it had a great deal to do with his indisposition. I think even the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) would not care to go too emphatically on record as being wholly satisfied with relations between British Columbia and his own department.
Then we have another minister of the crown writing west and saying that "the provincial government seem unable to meet the ordinary business conditions which the federal government found it necessary to impose in connection with relief administration." Again we find that very early in the session of the provincial legislature a member rose in his place and moved the adjournment of the house to call attention to the fact that the government were not even paying their relief bills. Relief orders had been given to country stores, and a rather unfortunate situation existed in that regard. I know that to be a fact within my own knowledge, for I went into a country store-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to quote someone who is responsible and not give hearsay in support of what he thinks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I certainly will not quote the hon. gentleman, for I do not think he is responsible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: You are taking up the time of the house with a lot of political nonsense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I might remind my hon. friend of this verse of the poet:
While broken teacups, wisely kept for show,
Rang'd o'er the chimney, glisten'd in a row,
I went into a country store, and the proprietor told me that his wholesaler was pressing him for cash, not an unusual thing in these days. The storekeeper had a stack of relief orders, all initialled and delivered, and he offered them to the wholesaler, but the wholesaler said, "I do not want them; I want cash." Again, we find the city council of North Vancouver, quite a large city, voting money to allow some delegates to take part in an unemployment parade to Victoria. They did so with the comment that they did not believe much in such parades, but they thought it was a good idea to take some steps to stir up the government at Victoria. Then we find the city council of Vancouver saying they did not think they could legally vote money for this purpose, although they would like to do so, but they gave these people relief while they were there and promised them all the flags they needed for their procession or parade. Again we find Senator McRae writing to North Vancouver, which he used to represent, and saying that the blame lay with the province rather than with the dominion.
I have still another example. The Vancouver Sun is known, of course, to be a Liberal newspaper, but it is no more a partisan Liberal newspaper than the Province is a partisan Conservative newspaper. The owner of that newspaper is reputed to be a man of wealth; at any rate he is abundantly able to defend any action for libel and to pay any expenses or damages which might be levied against him. A few months ago he came out in his newspaper with the announcement that he had detailed one of its editorial staff to make a personal investigation, extending from the coast to the Alberta boundary, and report his findings in connection with unemployment. I cannot read the whole report, though I should like to gratify my hon. friend opposite. I will only read three short sentences which are indicative of the whole situation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

Your stuff is all bunk, tha^ is all I have to tell you.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
"And the loud laugh that spoke the vacant mind." The article states:
British Columbia's grossest political scandal has been perpetrated under the guise of "unemployment relief."
Those words are actionable if they are not true.
In its morals the operation compares rather unfavourably with stealing pennies from the baby's bank. In its magnitude it more nearly resembles a Wall street raid.
The crime is this: that millions of dollars of public money purporting to be used in the relief and assistance of the needy and destitute, have been scattered broadcast in wages and purchases of supplies among political favourites. Meanwhile the hungry have remained unfed.
That is a statement which leaves the publisher completely open to a libel action, but nothing has been done about it. It is needless to go into details; I have not time, but at any rate, the whole thing was stopped because money ran short. In the meantime the province made a demand upon the dominion treasury; they said, "Give us half; give us your share of the money we have been squandering," but very much to the credit of the government of this dominion, they refused. They said, "No. We are willing to give our share of the money which you have spent on relief, but we are not going to spend our money on your wildcat camps, political friends, and so on." Then the fat was in the fire and the work had to be shut down instantly, and after that the government was reduced to the giving of as much direct relief as could be afforded. That is the very worst form of dole. Hon. members who have howled down any idea of unemployment insurance were only too pleased to see doles given out. Only two meals a day were given to men sitting in camp alongside a road, looking at the road which was in a disgraceful condition. I feel certain that if I had gone and said, "Boys, for God's sake fix that road at your own expense," they would have done it rather than have sat idly by and looked at it. But that was the situation: they were getting two meals a day for looking at it. That happened three months ago, and since then, about every third day we have received notice that work was going to start again, but nothing has been done. They are now talking of a scheme of giving them $7.50 a month, but even that does not seem to be in operation yet.
I repeat, what is needed is for the government to send a commissioner there with full power to investigate, not a political committee. The local government, to save their face-and there is mighty little of their face left in this regard-have appointed a political committee 
of their own choosing, in the proportion of seven to four. They could not even be content with a majority but they had to have seven out of eleven. And they were handpicked on their own side because they could not trust their men. Some of the Conservatives are up in arms about the situation I have outlined, and now a political whitewashing committee has been appointed to administer the necessary whitewash. That is not the kind of investigation we are entitled to, nor is it the kind this government are entitled to for their own protection and information.
It may be claimed that this is a provincial matter and that they have not been squandering the federal money. But much of the trouble that arose in all these months, with* which the Minister of Labour is at least partially familiar-because a lot of it happened in the time of his predecessor-was due to that very thing, that the province was trying to squander federal money, and the trouble came to a head when the federal government would not stand for it. It is the duty of this government to see that the dominion relief scheme is effective, and I am safe in saying that if they carry it out along these lines more than ninety per cent of the people of British Columbia will b,e grateful and more than grateful to them for doing so. Large sums of money are being spent. We have got into the habit of talking in millions, and the Dominion government are paying fifty per cent and in some cases more than that, so that it is their duty to investigate, not only the past, although a good deal of investigation would be necessary if we go into what has been done in the past, but what is being done now and what will be done in the future. There are months and months ahead of us during which we shall need relief from the Dominion government and steps should be taken to see that the money is properly spent.
I submit that it should be this man's duty to see that the money is spent wisely and efficiently so that good work will be done and value got for the money spent. Then he should have power to direct and to dominate, if you like, these misfits in Victoria in order to see that the work is done in such a way and under such conditions that the Dominion government can readily and without question pay their share of the expense. That will have the further great benefit of avoiding any delays, which are sometimes very unfortunate for the municipalities, whose funds are not ample. It is important that there shall be no delay in paying the dominion's share of the money. That is the primary duty of the government, and I hope they will send a good

Unemployment-Mr. MacMillan
man out. Secondly-and this is most important-he should see that the money is really received by the people who need work and who are hungry. Let me refer to the act passed last year. What is it intended to do?
It is for the purpose of relieving distress and providing employment; and elsewhere it speaks of the "speedy and unhampered prosecution of all relief measures". That is all I ask: that they send a man there who will see that the prosecution of the work is speedy and unhampered-unhampered by that bunch of curiosities in Victoria-for the relief of unemployed people. We shall not fulfil the purpose of the act under present conditions unless the government exercises greater supervision there.
In order that my attitude may be quite free from any appearance of partisanship I am going to join with my co-partner, or co-leader, or the other half of the independent desk- we will call it that rather than group or party-and vote against the want of confidence in the government. I hope, however, that the government will take steps to have these matters to which I have referred, carefully considered, and introduce methods that will improve conditions. They have given notice of an extension of the act under which relief is afforded and now will be the proper opportunity to provide more stringent regulations along the lines I have suggested in order that at least in the province of British Columbia, with which of course I am more familiar, the money will go from the federal authorities to the people who so badly need it.

speechtext:
In rising to say a word or two in connection with the amendment, I desire as the representative of a constituency in Saskatchewan to thank the government of the day for the most sympathetic manner in which they have come to the assistance of the people in that province. I was surprised at the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who tried to establish a comparison between conditions to-day and conditions in the year 1921 when he came into power. There is no comparison whatsoever. At that time I was in a business in Saskatchewan which I think reflected more quickly than any other the condition of unemployment or employment. That was the time of great deflation of commodity prices as a result of the war. During the war the price of almost every commodity had gone up from 50 to 200 per cent, and in twelve months prices dropped again practically to where they had been before, so that there was considerable dislocation of trade and some unemployment. But the situation then was by no means comparable to the present situation.
It is therefore a mistake to make any such comparison. In western Canada at that time there was no unemployment, or at least very little. Rentals, which are a fair index in the city I come from and in every other city and town in Saskatchewan, remained practically at the level that existed prior to 1921. It is different to-day. Rentals of business properties in that .part of the country are down from thirty-five to fifteen per cent.
The problem before us is a national and international problem; it is something over which the government has no control, and the leader of the opposition knows that perfectly well. The right hon. gentleman spoke about raising fears throughout the country because unemployment was rampant. I would ask hon gentlemen opposite this question: Last year did we not sit here week after week listening to wails of woe, particularly from members from western Canada in regard to conditions out in that country? We heard these wails of woe until we were all heartily sick of them, and now the right hon. gentleman comes along and says that we are creating fears in the minds of the people in connection with unemployment. I have wondered, while listening to this talk in regard to unemployment relief, just what the late government did from an administrative point of view. I wonder to what extent the lack of administrative vision has accentuated the unemployment which exists to-day? I could quote figures from my own city in regard to unemployment and the relief granted by federal, provincial and municipal authorities, but I do not intend to weary the house. However, I should like to read a letter from the provincial secretary of the Retail Merchants' Association of the province of Saskatchewan. This gentleman is a very staunch supporter of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). This letter, addressed to the Premier of Saskatchewan and dated Saskatoon, January 12, 1932, reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Anderson:
At the executive meeting of our association which we held in Regina on Thursday and Friday, January 14 and 15, and at which meeting we also had in attendance the directors of the Retailers' Trust Company, Limited, and the members of the southern merchandising committee of our association, the subject of the manner in which the distribution of relief by the federal and provincial governments, through the Saskatchewan relief commission, was pretty thoroughly talked over by the members present.	.	T
A resolution was unanimously passed that 1 should write you, expressing appreciation of the manner in which this relief has been carried

Unemployment-Mr. MacMillan
out by the governments, through the relief commission, and I was to say to you, Dr. Anderson, that, generally speaking, we believed it to he carried out in a very satisfactory manner, both to the recipients and to the retail trade, as well as to the citizens of Saskatchewan.
I was asked to send a copy of this letter to the Hon. R. B. Bennett, Hon. Robert Weir, and to Mr. Henry Black, chairman of the Saskatchewan relief commission.
I can assure you it affords me much pleasure personally, to write this letter.
Yours faithfully,
W. L. McQuarrie,
Provincial Secretary,
Retail Merchants' Association.
I could read other letters of a similar nature, but I will not take up the time of the house. I'am glad to see the Leader of the Opposition in his place, as well as the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). I regret that the former Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) is not present because I intend to refer to a matter which pertains to the constituencies of Prince Albert and North Battle-ford, and he might be interested in my remarks.
During the years from 1921 up to the time the natural resources were returned to the province a condition arose which was not in the best interests of the people of Saskatchewan. I refer to the manner in which timber permits were handed out to the friends of the late government, and also to the granting of tie contracts. I hold in my hand a list of the timber permits which have been granted to a firm in Prince Albert, friends of the right hon. gentleman, numbering in all some sixty-one or sixty-four. In each case these permits are listed as being fire-killed timber. They were granted from the year 1925 up to just prior to the last federal elections, and it is a strange thing that no one but this particular firm could obtain a permit to cut timber in this section of northern Saskatchewan. It is also a strange thing that apparently no one but this particular firm could obtain a contract from the Canadian National Railways for the supplying of railway ties. It looks very much like collusion between the Department of the Interior, the Canadian National Railways and the contractors in Prince Albert. Hon. members familiar with timber regulations know that fire-killed timber is that which has been run over by fire and fifty per cent of which will eventually die. The royalty for such timber is only fifty per cent of what it is for standing green timber, so that these contractors by being permitted to lease this as fire-killed timber have paid the government a much smaller royalty than would have been required had it been properly designated.

Q. Where?
A. At Montreal.
Q. Whom did you inquire from?
A. I was going through there and I inquired when them contracts would be given out.
Q. Whom did you inquire from?
A. To the office of the Canadian National Railways.
Q. Whom did you see?
A. I saw one of the clerks there.
Q. Did you know who he was?
A. No. He just asked me what I wanted and I asked him about the contracts and he told me that at that time in order to get a contract you had to speak to the sitting member in the House of Commons for North Battle-ford. ... I went there and inquired for a contract and he advised me the best way out of that was to see C. R. McIntosh. That is what he advised me to do.
